✅ قائمة فحص OSCE — تقييم الألم (20 نقطة)

  1. التقديم: رحّب بالمريض، عرّف بنفسك، تحقق من الهوية (معرّفان)

  2. الموافقة: اشرح الإجراء واحصل على موافقة شفهية

  3. نظافة اليدين: اغسل يديك / استخدم معقمًا كحوليًا

  4. الخصوصية: وفّر ستارة خصوصية إن لزم

  5. الوضعية: تأكد من راحة المريض والإضاءة الجيدة

  6. P — المثير/المخفف: "ما الذي يُحسّن/يُسوّئ الألم؟"

  7. Q — الصفة: "كيف تشعر به؟ حاد/خفيف/حارق؟"

  8. R — المنطقة/الانتشار: "أرني أين. هل ينتشر؟"

  9. S — الشدة: استخدم مقياسًا مناسبًا (NRS/VAS/FACES)

  10. T — الوقت: "مستمر أم متقطع؟ منذ متى؟"

  11. U — الفهم/التأثير: "كيف يؤثر على حياتك؟"

  12. العلاجات المنزلية: اسأل عمّا استُخدم من وسائل دوائية وغير دوائية

  13. الملاحظة السلوكية: تعبيرات الوجه، الحماية، وضعية الجسم

  14. العلامات الفسيولوجية: النبض، الضغط، التنفس، التعرق، الشحوب

  15. التوثيق: أكمل نموذج تقييم الألم

  16. تخطيط التدخلات: دوائية وغير دوائية

  17. تثقيف المريض: اشرح خطة إدارة الألم

  18. خطة إعادة التقييم: حدد متى ستُعاد التقييم (15/30 دقيقة)

  19. نظافة اليدين: اغسل يديك بعد ملامسة المريض

  20. الإبلاغ: أبلغ الطبيب بالنتائج إذا لزم الأمر

👨‍⚖️ نصائح لممتحن OSCE

افعل (درجات عالية): ابدأ بتقديم واضح وموافقة؛ حافظ على التواصل البصري؛ استخدم أسئلة مفتوحة أولًا؛ أظهر تعاطفًا ("يبدو هذا صعبًا")؛ استخدم كلمات المريض نفسها عند التوثيق؛ صدّق تقرير المريض الذاتي؛ اسأل عن التأثير على الوظائف اليومية؛ اذكر نتائجك بصوت مسموع؛ حدد خطة إعادة التقييم بوضوح؛ أدِّ نظافة اليدين بشكل ظاهر.

لا تفعل (فقدان درجات): تخطي التقديم أو الموافقة؛ استخدام مصطلحات طبية لا يفهمها المريض؛ الشك في ألم المريض أو التقليل منه؛ تقدير الألم بصريًا دون مقياس؛ التسرع في PQRSTU؛ نسيان الملاحظة غير اللفظية؛ تخطي نظافة اليدين؛ التركيز فقط على الرقم؛ تجاهل العوامل الثقافية؛ عدم توثيق إعادة التقييم.

عبارات تواصل تكسب الدرجات: "أتفهم أنك تعاني من ألم، دعني أساعدك." · "على مقياس من 0 إلى 10، حيث 0 لا يوجد ألم و10 أسوأ ألم يمكن تخيله، ما الرقم الذي تعطيه لألمك الآن؟" · "هل يمكنك وصف الألم بكلماتك؟" · "هل هناك ما يُحسّنه أو يُسوّئه؟" · "كيف يؤثر هذا الألم على أنشطتك اليومية؟" · "سأعود خلال 30 دقيقة للاطمئنان عليك."

إدارة الوقت: محطة OSCE النموذجية 7-10 دقائق. وزّعها تقريبًا: دقيقة للتقديم والموافقة، 4-5 دقائق لتقييم PQRSTU، دقيقة للملاحظة، 1-2 دقيقة للتوثيق/الخطة، دقيقة للختام وخطة إعادة التقييم.

🧠 وسائل الحفظ والاختصارات

PQRSTU: تخيّل جملة "الناس يسألون عن معاناة حقيقية ليفهموها بصدق" — كل كلمة تقابل حرفًا: مثير/مخفف، صفة، منطقة/انتشار، شدة، وقت، فهم/تأثير.

FLACC: تخيّل طفلًا رضيعًا — راقب وجهه، انظر لساقيه، لاحظ نشاطه، استمع لبكائه، حاول تهدئته.

QUESTT (الأطفال): اسأل الطفل (إن كان قادرًا على الكلام) والوالد (دائمًا)؛ استخدم مقاييس مناسبة؛ قيّم السلوك والتغيرات الفسيولوجية؛ أشرك الوالد؛ راعِ السبب؛ اتخذ إجراءً وقيّم النتائج.

جرعة الأفيون الزائدة — "الثلاثية P": حدقة ضيقة جدًا (Pinpoint pupils)، تنفس ضعيف (RR <10)، وعي ضعيف (هبوط مستوى الوعي). العلاج: نالوكسون (Narcan) 0.4-2 ملغ وريدي/عضلي.

أنواع الألم: حاد (مفاجئ، أقل من 30 يومًا) · مزمن (أكثر من 3-6 أشهر) · استقبالي (تلف نسيجي) · جسدي (جلد/عظم/عضلة) · حشوي (أعضاء) · عصبي (حارق/طاعن) · مُحال (موضع بعيد، مثل احتشاء القلب ← الفك) · وهمي (طرف مبتور).

🗂️ بطاقات المراجعة السريعة

س: عرّف الألم وفق IASP (2020)؟ ج: تجربة حسية وعاطفية غير سارة مرتبطة بتلف نسيجي فعلي أو محتمل.
س: مراحل مسار الألم الأربع؟ ج: التحويل ← النقل ← الإدراك ← التعديل.
س: أفضل أداة لمريض ICU موصول بجهاز تنفس؟ ج: CPOT (0-8)؛ درجة أكبر من 2 = ألم كبير.
س: فئات FLACC؟ ج: الوجه، الساقان، النشاط، البكاء، القابلية للتهدئة (0-2 لكل بند، المجموع 0-10).
س: متى تُعاد التقييم بعد مسكن وريدي؟ ج: 15 دقيقة (ذروة التأثير).
س: متى تُعاد التقييم بعد مسكن فموي؟ ج: 30 دقيقة (ذروة التأثير).
س: الدرجة الأولى في سلم WHO؟ ج: غير أفيوني (باراسيتامول، مضادات التهاب) ± مساعدات.
س: الدرجة الثالثة في سلم WHO؟ ج: أفيوني قوي (مورفين، فنتانيل) + غير أفيوني ± مساعدات.
س: ثالوث جرعة الأفيون الزائدة؟ ج: معدل تنفس أقل من 10، حدقة ضيقة، هبوط وعي. الترياق: نالوكسون.
س: ماذا يعني QUESTT؟ ج: اسأل، استخدم، قيّم، أشرك الوالد، راعِ السبب، اتخذ إجراءً.
س: نظرية البوابة — السنة والمؤلفان؟ ج: 1965، ميلزاك ووول.
س: أفضل مقياس لمريض خرف؟ ج: PAINAD (0-10) — أداة ملاحظة.

📚 ملخص مراجعة الامتحانات — أهم 20 نقطة

  1. تعريف IASP: تجربة حسية وعاطفية غير سارة مع تلف نسيجي

  2. الألم = العلامة الحيوية الخامسة (الجوينت كوميشن)

  3. المعيار الذهبي: تقرير المريض الذاتي

  4. مسار الألم: التحويل ← النقل ← الإدراك ← التعديل

  5. نظرية البوابة: ميلزاك ووول (1965)

  6. مقياس البالغين: NRS (0-10)، الأكثر شيوعًا

  7. أطفال أقل من 3 سنوات: FLACC

  8. أطفال 3-8 سنوات: Wong-Baker FACES

  9. ICU موصول بجهاز تنفس: CPOT (المعيار الذهبي)

  10. الخرف: PAINAD

  11. تفسير الدرجات: 0-3 خفيف، 4-6 متوسط، 7-10 شديد (طوارئ عند 8-10)

  12. إعادة التقييم: 15 دقيقة بعد الوريدي، 30 دقيقة بعد الفموي

  13. سلم WHO: غير أفيوني ← أفيوني ضعيف ← أفيوني قوي

  14. PQRSTU: مثير-صفة-منطقة-شدة-وقت-فهم

  15. QUESTT: اسأل-استخدم-قيّم-أشرك-راعِ-اتخذ (أطفال)

  16. الألم العصبي: حارق، طاعن، كهربائي

  17. الألم الاستقبالي: خفيف مستمر، مؤلم بشكل ثابت

  18. جرعة الأفيون الزائدة: تنفس <10 + حدقة ضيقة + ↓وعي ← نالوكسون

  19. الألم المُحال: ألم صدر ← فك (احتشاء)؛ ألم كتف (حجاب حاجز)

  20. الألم الوهمي: ألم حقيقي في طرف مبتور

أكثر المفاهيم اختبارًا في NCLEX/بروميتريك: تقرير المريض الذاتي هو المعيار الذهبي؛ توقيت إعادة التقييم (15/30 دقيقة)؛ اختيار المقياس الصحيح حسب العمر/الحالة؛ درجات سلم WHO للمسكنات؛ سلامة الأفيونات وإدارة الجرعة الزائدة؛ التدخلات غير الدوائية (نظرية البوابة).

🎓 نصائح امتحانات الترخيص (NCLEX/بروميتريك)

أولويات تقييم الألم: صدّق المريض دائمًا — تقريره الذاتي هو المعيار الذهبي؛ قيّم قبل أن تتدخل؛ أعطِ الأولوية للاحتياجات الفسيولوجية (ماسلو) — الألم يؤثر على السلامة و ABCs؛ جرّب التدخلات غير الدوائية أولًا للألم الخفيف (دعم نظرية البوابة)؛ الجمع بين الدوائي وغير الدوائي يعطي أفضل نتيجة؛ أعد التقييم بعد كل تدخل — أمر حاسم للنجاح؛ لا تُفوّض تقييم الألم أبدًا لطاقم غير مرخص — يتطلب حكمًا تمريضيًا؛ احترم اختلاف التعبير الثقافي عن الألم.

تركيز امتحان بروميتريك (مصر/الخليج): تطبيق سلم WHO للمسكنات، اختيار المقياس الصحيح للفئة السكانية، معايير التوثيق، ألم الأطفال (FLACC، Wong-Baker)، إدارة الألم بعد الجراحة، الاعتبارات الثقافية والدينية.

أسئلة الفخ الشائعة: السؤال يطلب "الأولوية" — السلامة أولًا، ثم الألم؛ فخ: افتراض أن العلامات الحيوية وحدها تعكس دقة الألم (خطأ)؛ فخ: اختيار مقياس خاطئ للعمر؛ فخ: إعطاء مسكن دون خطة إعادة تقييم؛ فخ: عدم تصديق تقرير المريض الذاتي.

استراتيجية حل الأسئلة: اقرأ نص السؤال بعناية — حدد العمر والمكان والحالة؛ ابحث عن كلمات مفتاحية ("الأولوية"، "الإجراء الأول"، "الأنسب")؛ طبّق ماسلو — الفسيولوجي قبل النفسي؛ طبّق ABC — المجرى الهوائي، التنفس، الدورة قبل الألم؛ اختر التقييم قبل التدخل إلا في الطوارئ؛ اختر تقرير المريض بدلًا من ملاحظة الممرض؛ اختر النهج المنهجي (PQRSTU) بدلًا من الأسئلة العشوائية.

❓ الأسئلة الشائعة

س: ماذا لو رفض المريض تقييم ألمه برقم؟ احترم اختياره واستخدم الملاحظة السلوكية بدلًا من ذلك. وثّق "رفض المريض التقييم الرقمي" وصف العلامات الملاحظة (تكشير، حماية، تغيرات العلامات الحيوية).

س: كم مرة يجب إعادة تقييم الألم؟ كل 4 ساعات كحد أدنى بالمستشفى؛ بعد 15 دقيقة من مسكن وريدي؛ بعد 30 دقيقة من مسكن فموي؛ بعد أي إجراء؛ كلما اشتكى المريض.

س: ماذا لو قيّم المريض ألمه 10/10 لكنه يبدو مرتاحًا؟ صدّق المريض — الألم تجربة ذاتية، والعوامل الثقافية والنفسية تؤثر على طريقة التعبير عنه. لا تقل أبدًا "لا تبدو وكأنك تتألم."

س: هل يمكنني تقدير الألم بصريًا دون مقياس؟ لا. استخدم دائمًا مقاييس معتمدة. تقدير الممرض البصري غير موثوق وفق الأبحاث (Powell et al.).

س: أي مقياس لمريض يتحدث لغة مختلفة؟ Wong-Baker FACES (لا يحتاج لغة) أو NRS مترجم. مخطط الجسم يساعد في تحديد الموضع.

س: متى أتصل بالطبيب بخصوص الألم؟ درجة 7-10، بداية شديدة مفاجئة، عدم استجابة للمسكن، ألم جديد منتشر، أو علامات حمراء مصاحبة (ألم صدر، ضيق تنفس، تغير الوعي).

س: ما الجرعة اليومية القصوى للباراسيتامول؟ البالغون: 4 غرام/يوم (4000 ملغ). كبار السن أو مرضى الكبد: 2-3 غرام/يوم — تحقق دائمًا.

س: كيف أقيّم الألم لمريض في غيبوبة؟ استخدم مقاييس سلوكية — CPOT (في ICU)، أو FLACC، أو PAINAD — وراقب التكشير، الحماية، تغيرات النبض/الضغط/التنفس، والتململ.

س: هل يمكنني إعطاء مسكن إضافي إذا بقيت الدرجة مرتفعة بعد إعادة التقييم؟ اتبع أمر الطبيب. إذا استمر الألم فوق 4 رغم الجرعة القصوى، اتصل بالطبيب لأوامر جديدة وفكّر في نهج متعدد الوسائط.

🧠 اختبر نفسك — اختيار من متعدد

اختر إجابة لكل سؤال، وهتظهرلك الإجابة الصح فورًا بعد اختيارك.

[[MCQ_QUIZ]]

✅ اختبر نفسك — صح أم خطأ

اضغط "صح" أو "خطأ"، وهيظهرلك التفسير فورًا.

[[TF_QUIZ]]

📝 أكمل الفراغ

حاول تتذكر الإجابة، وبعدين اضغط لإظهار الحل.

[[FB_QUIZ]]

🌟 أهم النقاط

  1. صدّق المريض — تقريره الذاتي هو المعيار الذهبي

  2. الألم هو العلامة الحيوية الخامسة — قيّمه بشكل منهجي

  3. استخدم مقاييس معتمدة للفئة المناسبة

  4. أعد التقييم بعد كل تدخل (15 أو 30 دقيقة)

  5. المسكنات متعددة الوسائط تعمل بشكل أفضل

  6. التدخلات غير الدوائية تدعم الدوائية (نظرية البوابة)

  7. ضع في الاعتبار الفئات الخاصة: أطفال، مسنين، ICU، حوامل

  8. وثّق بدقة باستخدام كلمات المريض نفسها

  9. تعرّف على العلامات الحمراء التي تتطلب تدخلاً عاجلاً

  10. ادعم إدارة الألم المناسبة — إنه حق للمريض

رسالة أخيرة من المؤلف: تقييم الألم ليس مجرد مهمة — إنه فعل رحمة. في كل مرة تخصص فيها الوقت لتقييم ألم المريض بشكل صحيح، أنت تُصدّق تجربته وتُقدم له الرعاية التي يستحقها. لا تُهمل أبدًا، لا تشك أبدًا. فقط استمع، لاحظ، وثّق، وتصرف.

title_en: Pain Assessment — The Complete Nursing Guide
content_en:
🎯 Learning Objectives

Cognitive Objectives (Knowledge):

  • Define pain according to the IASP (2020) revised definition.
  • Identify the four stages of the pain pathway: transduction, transmission, perception, and modulation.
  • Classify pain types: acute vs. chronic, nociceptive vs. neuropathic, somatic vs. visceral vs. referred vs. phantom.
  • Explain the Gate Control Theory of Pain and its clinical significance.
  • List validated assessment tools: NRS, VAS, VDS, Wong-Baker FACES, CPOT, BPS, FLACC, TVP, PAINAD, Pain Thermometer, APCA POS.
  • Describe the PQRSTU / OPQRST / OLDCARTS mnemonics for pain history.
  • Differentiate between subjective and objective pain data.
  • Describe pain manifestations: pallor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea, anxiety, clenched fists, restlessness.
  • Recall the QUESTT approach for pediatric pain assessment.
  • Explain the WHO Analgesic Ladder and multimodal analgesia.

💪 Psychomotor Objectives (Skills):

  • Perform systematic pain assessment using the PQRSTU format.
  • Select the most appropriate pain scale per patient type and age.
  • Document pain accurately using standardized formats.
  • Reassess pain 15 minutes post-IV and 30 minutes post-oral analgesic.
  • Recognize non-verbal pain cues in ICU, pediatric, and dementia patients.
  • Apply the FLACC scale for children under 3 years.
  • Use the CPOT/BPS for intubated ICU patients.
  • Perform comprehensive assessment including behavioral and physiological indicators.
  • Use body diagrams to locate pain areas.
  • Provide non-pharmacological interventions based on Gate Control Theory.

🎯 Affective Objectives:

  • Appreciate pain as "the 5th vital sign."
  • Accept the patient's self-report as the gold standard.
  • Advocate for adequate pain management.
  • Show empathy and cultural sensitivity.
  • Avoid undertreating or overtreating pain.
  • Understand pain assessment is NOT an academic exercise — every question provides essential information.

⚡ Quick Facts

Pain severity scale: 0–3 no therapy change · 4–7 change analgesic · 8–10 pain emergency.

💡 The Golden Rule of Pain Assessment: Pain is subjective. The patient's self-report is always the gold standard. "Pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, existing whenever the person says it does." (McCaffery, 1968)

📊 Evidence-Based Practice

📚 Key Foundational Guidelines:

  • The IASP (2020) redefined pain as: "An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage." (Raja et al., 2020)
  • Joint Commission (2017) standards require pain assessment at every clinical encounter and documentation of reassessment within 30–60 minutes of any intervention.
  • WHO Analgesic Ladder (1986, updated 2019): an evidence-based framework for stepwise pain management — non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid.
  • PADIS Guidelines (2018) from the Society of Critical Care Medicine recommend CPOT as the preferred tool for ICU pain assessment in non-verbal patients.
  • Effective clinical management of pain depends on its accurate assessment, entailing a comprehensive evaluation of pain, symptoms, functional status, and clinical history.
  • Pain assessment is an ongoing process — not an isolated event. Intervention effectiveness must be evaluated via subsequent assessments.

Landmark Studies in Pain Assessment

🏆 Best Practice Summary:

  • Use multimodal analgesia (non-pharmacological + pharmacological).
  • Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA) reduces anxiety and improves satisfaction.
  • Assess pain at least every 4 hours in hospital.
  • Use validated scales — never estimate visually.
  • Reassess after intervention (15 min IV / 30 min oral).
  • Always accept the patient's self-report.

6 Rules for Effective Pain Assessment (Powell et al., IASP)

What can be done to ensure an effective pain assessment process?

1. Accept the patient's self-reported pain as accurate. Pain is an inherently subjective experience influenced by multiple factors (gender differences, socially acceptable pain thresholds, culturally acceptable levels of "complaining," hopelessness, diminished morale, coping abilities, and the meaning attached to the pain). Accept the patient as an expert on their own body. While some patients may exaggerate their pain, this will generally be the exception — a provider's observational report cannot be assumed to be an accurate indicator of the patient's pain.

2. Allow patients to describe their pain in their own words. Socially acceptable answers demand a sensitive exploration. For patients uncomfortable expressing themselves, provide a sample of relevant words on cards from which they can select the most appropriate descriptors. The primary intention is to listen to the patient rather than make false assumptions.

3. Listen actively to what the patient says. Focus attention on the patient, observe behavioral and body language, and paraphrase words when necessary to ensure clear understanding. In emotionally charged encounters, actively listen for nonverbal descriptors.

4. Use body diagrams to locate the pain. Show the patient a picture of the human body (front and back), ask them to indicate primary and multiple areas of pain, and demonstrate the direction of any radiated pain.

5. Use pain scales to measure severity. Pain scales, of varying complexity, can be used to determine the severity of the expressed pain.

6. Diagnose the cause and treat. While it's important to manage pain as soon as possible, also diagnose the cause of the pain and treat it if possible, ensuring longer-term resolution.

⏱️ How Long Should Assessment Take? Time varies according to individual patients and clinic demands. Patients in severe pain may be unable to provide meaningful information, so assessment may need to be brief (intensity, quality, location) so pain management can be provided quickly. It is the quality of the pain assessment, not the quantity of time, that results in effective pain management.

📖 Introduction

Pain is an unpleasant sensation and emotional experience that links to tissue damage. Pain is one of the most common reasons patients seek medical care, yet it remains one of the most undertreated conditions in clinical settings worldwide. As nurses, we serve as the primary assessors and advocates for our patients' pain experience.

Pain affects every aspect of a patient's well-being: it disrupts sleep, delays wound healing, causes respiratory complications (splinting), increases stress hormones, leads to anxiety and depression, and significantly impairs quality of life.

The Joint Commission recognized pain as the "5th Vital Sign" to emphasize that it must be assessed as routinely and systematically as temperature, pulse, respiration, and blood pressure.

Where pain levels permit, the assessment process is essentially a dialogue between the patient and the health care provider that addresses the nature, location, and extent of the pain, its impact on daily life, and treatment options.

🚨 The Cost of Unmanaged Pain — Clinical Consequences:

  • Delayed recovery and wound healing
  • Pneumonia risk (from splinting)
  • DVT and pulmonary embolism
  • Prolonged ICU stay
  • Chronic pain development
  • Increased mortality

📘 Definition — Official IASP Definition (2020)

📚 Official Definition (IASP 2020):

"An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage."

— International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP), 2020 — Raja, S.N. et al., Pain, 161(9), 1976–1982.

💡 Don't Let Anyone Define Pain but the Patient: Pain is subjective — the patient's self-report is always the gold standard when they can communicate. Never doubt the patient's pain report. "Pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, existing whenever the person says it does." (McCaffery, 1968)

Related Pain Terminology

TermDefinition
NociceptionNeural process of encoding noxious stimuli
AllodyniaPain from a non-painful stimulus
HyperalgesiaIncreased response to a painful stimulus
AnalgesiaAbsence of pain in response to a stimulus
ParesthesiaAbnormal sensation (tingling)

🔀 Types & Sources of Pain (Complete Classification)

  • Acute Pain: Sudden, severe, short-term; typically heals within 30 days (e.g., a new bruise).
  • Chronic Pain: Recurring pain lasting more than 3–6 months (e.g., long-term back pain).
  • Referred Pain: Felt at a site distant from the injury and does not follow a peripheral nerve path (e.g., jaw pain during a heart attack).
  • Phantom Pain: Real pain felt in a limb that is no longer there.
  • Physiological Pain: Results from potential tissue damage.
  • Somatic Pain: From superficial tissues (skin, bone, muscle, joints).
  • Visceral Pain: From internal organs (heart, stomach, liver) — deep and cramping.
  • Neuropathic Pain: From nerve cell changes; described as burning, shooting, or electrical.
  • Radiating Pain: Follows a defined peripheral nerve path.

📅 Classification by Duration

TypeDurationExample
Acute< 30 daysPost-op, trauma
Chronic> 3–6 monthsArthritis
RecurrentEpisodicMigraine

⚙️ Classification by Mechanism

TypeOriginCharacter
NociceptiveTissue damageDull, aching

💎 Diagnostic Pearls — Pain Quality Reveals Etiology:

  • "Burning, shooting, electrical" → neuropathic pain
  • "Dull, aching" → nociceptive pain
  • "Terrible, unbearable" → affective valuation more than a physical descriptor
  • Worse in early morning hours → inflammation
  • Constant high pain → chronic pain disease
  • Decreases with movement → possible osteoarthritis
  • Only rest relieves it → chronic pain needing cognitive restructuring

💡 Localization — The Most Important Question: Localization may be the single most important question in pain assessment — it can differentiate a radicular from a nonradicular etiology. These are only rough indicators; further questioning and examination are needed to confirm any suspicion.

🚪 Gate Control Theory of Pain

Proposed by Melzack & Wall (1965), this theory explains how non-painful stimuli can override and reduce the perception of pain:

  1. Gates are built into normal pain pathways.
  2. When gates open, the pain impulse is transmitted to the brain.
  3. When gates close, the pain impulse is reduced or blocked.

💡 Clinical Application: This theory is the scientific basis for non-pharmacological interventions such as massage, heat/cold therapy, TENS units, and distraction techniques to "close the gate" and reduce pain perception.

🔓 Gate-Closing Interventions (Non-Pharmacological)

  • Massage — activates large nerve fibers
  • Heat / cold therapy
  • TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation)
  • Distraction (music, TV, conversation)
  • Guided imagery / meditation
  • Deep breathing exercises
  • Positioning & repositioning

⚠️ Pain Manifestations

Common Signs & Symptoms

  • Pallor
  • Diaphoresis (sweating)
  • Tachycardia (HR over 100)
  • High blood pressure (over 140 systolic)
  • Nausea & vomiting (acute pain)
  • Fainting / dizziness (acute pain)
  • Anxiety / fear (chronic pain or trauma)
  • Clenched fists
  • Restlessness

Physiological Responses to Pain: Early in acute pain, the sympathetic nervous system is stimulated, causing:

  • Increased blood pressure
  • Increased pulse rate
  • Increased respiration
  • Pallor
  • Diaphoresis
  • Pupil dilation

🗣️ Behavioral Effects — Objective Assessment

  • Assess verbalization, vocal response, facial and body movements, and social interaction.
  • Facial expression is often the first indication of pain and may be the only manifestation in non-verbal patients.
  • Vocalizations such as moaning, groaning, crying, and screaming are associated with pain.

🧭 The 4 Pillars of Nursing Assessment

⚠️

💊

📍

👁️

Nursing Assessment includes: (1) Assess risk for pain (invasive procedures, anxious patients); (2) Response to previous pharmacological interventions; (3) Examine site of pain/discomfort; (4) Assess physical, behavioral and emotional signs (moaning, decreased activity, restlessness, irritability).

❗ Importance of Accurate Pain Assessment

The effective clinical management of pain ultimately depends on its accurate assessment (Powell et al.). Accurate pain assessment is critical because it:

  • Directs treatment decisions — intensity guides intervention: 0–3 no change, 4–7 change analgesic, 8–10 emergency.
  • Prevents complications of unmanaged pain: chronic pain, depression, sleep disturbances.
  • Identifies etiology — quality descriptors differentiate neuropathic from nociceptive pain.
  • Evaluates treatment effectiveness through reassessment.
  • Improves patient satisfaction and quality of life.
  • Prevents undertreatment — especially in the elderly, cognitively impaired, and non-verbal.
  • Prevents overtreatment — avoiding opioid dependency and adverse effects.
  • Is a legal & ethical obligation — pain management is a fundamental patient right (Joint Commission).

🚨 Consequences of Poor Pain Assessment:

  • Increased morbidity & mortality
  • Prolonged hospital stay
  • Development of chronic pain syndromes
  • Delayed wound healing (↑ cortisol)
  • Immunosuppression
  • Psychological distress (anxiety, depression)
  • Patient distrust of the healthcare system
  • Sleep deprivation
  • Reduced quality of life

✅ Benefits of Accurate Assessment:

  • Improved patient outcomes (+40%)
  • Reduced opioid consumption (30–50%)
  • Faster recovery times
  • Better patient satisfaction scores
  • Reduced healthcare costs
  • Compliance with Joint Commission standards

Sources: RNAO (2013); WHO (2019); Joint Commission Standards (2017)

💡 Key Message: Pain assessment is NOT an academic exercise! Every question provides essential information about etiology and the first steps to treat it. (Powell et al., Pearls of Wisdom)

🧠 The Pain Pathway — 4 Stages (Anatomy & Physiology)

The pain pathway consists of 4 sequential stages:

  1. Transduction: Conversion of a noxious stimulus (thermal, mechanical, chemical) into an electrical signal by nociceptors at the site of injury.
  2. Transmission: Propagation of the signal along afferent nerve fibers (A-delta & C fibers) from peripheral tissue → spinal cord → brain (thalamus).
  3. Perception: Conscious awareness and interpretation of pain in the cerebral cortex — where the "pain experience" is generated.
  4. Modulation: Descending pathways release endogenous opioids (endorphins, enkephalins) and neurotransmitters (serotonin, norepinephrine) to inhibit or amplify pain signals.
A-delta fibers

Myelinated, fast, sharp/localized pain (first pain)

C fibers

Unmyelinated, slow, dull/aching/burning pain (second pain)

A-beta fibers

Large myelinated, touch/pressure — activates Gate Control mechanism

📖 Additional Essential Terminology

TermDefinition
NociceptorSensory receptor that responds to painful stimuli
HypoalgesiaDecreased sensitivity to painful stimulus
DysesthesiaUnpleasant abnormal sensation
NeuralgiaPain in the distribution of a nerve

🗣️ Subjective Data Collection

Pain assessment includes subjective and objective data. Subjective data has 4 key components:

  • 1. Pain History: Give the patient the chance to describe, in their own words, how they view their pain and situation.
  • 2. Onset & Duration: When did it begin? How long has it lasted? Same time each day? How often?
  • 3. Location: Where exactly is it felt? Does it change with circumstances? Unilateral or bilateral? Ask the patient to point to the site.
  • 4. Intensity: A pain intensity scale (numerical, descriptive, or visual analog) is an easy, reliable way to determine intensity.

👁️ Objective Assessment

Objective assessment includes two major components:

1. Behavioral Effects: verbalization, vocal response, facial and body movements, and social interaction. Facial expression is often the first indication of pain.

2. Physiological Responses: early in acute pain, the sympathetic nervous system is stimulated, causing increased blood pressure, pulse, respiration, pallor, diaphoresis, and pupil dilation.

⚠️ Important Warning: Evidence suggests that health care providers' observational pain report cannot be assumed to be an accurate indicator of the patient's pain. Always trust the patient's self-report as the gold standard when they can communicate. (Powell et al.)

🧰 Adult Pain Assessment Tools — Full Details

Detailed description of adult pain assessment tools (from Powell et al., IASP Guide to Pain Management in Low-Resource Settings):

1. Visual Analogue Scale (VAS)

  • A 10-cm horizontal line anchored by "No pain" and "Worst pain imaginable." The patient marks the point reflecting their pain.
  • Advantages: Quick, simple, easy to score and compare, extensively validated, one of the best tools for tracking change.
  • Disadvantages: Highly sensitive to change; some adults find it too abstract; problematic with cognitive dysfunction, immediately post-op, and visual impairment.

2. Numerical Rating Scale (NRS)

  • Patient rates pain intensity from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable).
  • Can be administered verbally — overcomes visual or physical impairment issues.
  • Advantages: Quick, simple, easy to document and compare, well validated, translatable, detects treatment effect, easy to teach.
  • Disadvantages: Some patients can't complete it with verbal instructions alone; less reliable at age extremes and with non-verbal or cognitively impaired patients.

3. Verbal Descriptor Scale (VDS)

  • Patient chooses a descriptor: "No pain," "Mild pain," "Moderate pain," "Severe pain," "Very severe pain," "Worst pain possible."
  • Advantages: Quick, simple, easily comprehended, well validated, intuitively preferred by many patients.
  • Disadvantages: Depends on language interpretation; challenging across cultures; problematic for the very young/old, cognitively impaired, and illiterate.

Source: Powell, R.A. et al. Guide to Pain Management in Low-Resource Settings (IASP), Appendix 2.

4. APCA African Palliative Outcome Scale (APCA POS)

A multidimensional scale (0–5) that includes pain among other domains, used in palliative care and promoted by the WHO. It can be completed using a "hand scale" (closed fist = no pain to five open fingers = worst pain).

5. Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia (PAINAD)

An observational tool for dementia patients who cannot self-report verbally. It has 5 items (breathing, negative vocalization, facial expression, body language, consolability), each scored 0–2, for a total of 0–10.

✅ Indications for Pain Assessment

  • Every clinical encounter (per Joint Commission standards)
  • Before and after invasive procedures (IV insertion, wound care, dressing changes)
  • Post-operatively (after anesthesia recovery)
  • Before and after administration of analgesic medications
  • When the patient reports discomfort or shows behavioral signs
  • During routine nursing rounds (minimum every 4 hours in hospital)
  • When the patient has a history of chronic pain
  • When risk factors are present: anxiety, depression, previous trauma
  • In the ICU: continuously for intubated/non-verbal patients using CPOT/BPS
  • During palliative and end-of-life care
  • Before and after physical therapy or rehabilitation sessions
  • When the patient is admitted with acute trauma or injury

⚠️ Contraindications & Challenges

  • Patient unable to communicate (intubated, unconscious, severe cognitive impairment)
  • Language barriers between patient and provider
  • Cultural differences in pain expression (some cultures suppress it)
  • Age-related challenges: neonates need behavioral observation only; toddlers may show regressive behavior; preschoolers may view pain as punishment; adolescents may deny pain in front of peers
  • Dementia/Alzheimer's: unable to self-report — relies on PAINAD observation
  • Psychological conditions: depression, anxiety, PTSD may alter reporting
  • Medication effects: prior analgesics or sedation affecting response
  • Time constraints: emergencies requiring rapid assessment

⚠️ Important

For patients with dementia, the main rule is to ask directly about pain. For those with sufficient cognitive function, increase text size, include relatives, and avoid mental overload.

🧰 Preparation & Equipment

  • Appropriate pain scale: matched to the patient's age, development, and comprehension (NRS, VAS, Wong-Baker, FLACC, CPOT, PAINAD)
  • Privacy screen: as needed for comfort and confidentiality
  • Patient case sheet: for documenting findings
  • Good lighting: for accurate observation of facial/body expressions
  • Body diagram: for the patient to indicate primary and multiple pain locations

🩺 Nursing Procedure — 8 Steps

  1. Explain the procedure to the patient. (Promotes compliance, builds trust, reduces anxiety)
  2. Wash hands and wear gloves if needed. (Infection control)
  3. Provide privacy if needed. (Comfort, dignity, confidentiality)
  4. Ensure adequate lighting. (For accurate assessment of facial/body expressions)
  5. Assess pain severity using PQRSTU and choose the scale appropriate to the patient's age.
  6. Ask about remedial measures taken at home and in hospital (pharmacological and non-pharmacological) — to guide care and avoid duplication.
  7. Record findings on the pain assessment form. (Evidence of care, supports documentation)
  8. Perform hand hygiene and discard gloves. (Infection control)

📝 Documentation & Recording

Record and report the character of pain before intervention, therapies used, and the patient's response. This creates a complete clinical picture for continuity of care.

🖊️ Sample Documentation

Patient: [Name] | Date: [Date] | Time: [Time]
Pain Assessment:
• Location: Lumbar region of back (constant)
• Quality: Dull, aching (not radiating)
• Severity: 6/10 — Moderate pain
• Timing: Continuous; increases with mild physical activity
• Aggravating: Physical activity
• Relieving: Hot water bag applied
• Intervention: T. Dolo 650mg administered per doctor's order
• Reassessment: to be done at 30 min (oral) / 15 min (IV)
Note: Pain does not radiate; increases with mild activity.

Source: Devisri, R. — PPT Pain Assessment & Management (Sample Documentation)

💡 Scientific Rationales — Why We Do What We Do

  1. Explain procedure → Reduces anxiety, promotes cooperation, and builds therapeutic rapport. Anxious patients report higher pain scores (biopsychosocial model).
  2. Hand hygiene → Prevents healthcare-associated infections (HAIs). Proper hand hygiene reduces HAIs by up to 50% (CDC).
  3. Privacy → Respects patient dignity and encourages honest pain reporting; studies show patients underreport pain in public settings.
  4. Good lighting → Facial expression is often the first indication of pain and may be the only manifestation in non-verbal patients (Devisri, R.).
  5. Use PQRSTU → A systematic approach ensures no critical aspect is missed (Bates 1991; Powell et al., IASP).
  6. Ask about home remedies → Prevents medication duplication, identifies non-pharmacological effectiveness, informs the multimodal analgesia plan (WHO 2019).
  7. Document accurately → Creates a legal record, ensures continuity of care, and allows comparison over time; Joint Commission requires reassessment within 30–60 min of intervention.
  8. Reassessment timing → IV analgesics peak in 15 min; oral analgesics peak in 30 min. Reassessing at these times determines efficacy and the need for adjustment.

💡 Practical Nursing Tips

  • Believe the patient — never dismiss a pain report
  • Assess pain at every vital signs check (the 5th vital sign)
  • Reassess after each intervention (15 min IV / 30 min PO)
  • Use the same scale consistently for reliable comparison
  • Watch facial expression — it's often the first sign
  • Ask open-ended questions: "Tell me about your pain"
  • Show empathy — therapeutic communication reduces pain perception
  • Include the patient in the pain management plan
  • Use body diagrams for multiple pain sites
  • Consider cultural factors in pain expression
  • Combine pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches
  • Document the specific descriptors used by the patient

✨ Pearl of Wisdom

Pain assessment is NOT an academic exercise! Every question potentially provides essential information about the etiology of pain and the first steps to treat it. (Powell et al., Pearls of Wisdom, IASP)

📋 Complete Documentation Standards

Every pain assessment must document:

  • Date & time of assessment
  • Location (specific anatomical site, body diagram if multiple)
  • Quality/character (patient's own words: burning, aching, sharp, dull)
  • Intensity (numerical score using a validated tool: NRS 0–10)
  • Duration (continuous, intermittent, episodic)
  • Onset (sudden vs. gradual)
  • Aggravating & relieving factors
  • Associated symptoms (nausea, sweating, restlessness)
  • Impact on function (sleep, ADLs, mood)
  • Interventions performed (pharm & non-pharm)
  • Response to intervention (reassessment score after 15–30 min)
  • Patient education provided
  • Nurse signature

Source: Joint Commission Standards (2017); RNAO Best Practice Guidelines (2013).

🧼 Infection Control During Pain Assessment

  • Hand hygiene before and after patient contact (WHO 5 Moments of Hand Hygiene)
  • Use alcohol-based hand rub if hands are not visibly soiled
  • Wash hands with soap and water if visibly soiled or after contact with body fluids
  • Wear gloves if contact with wounds, dressings, or body fluids is expected
  • Change gloves between patients — never reuse
  • Clean pain assessment tools (rulers, cards, tablets) between patients
  • Follow standard precautions for all patients regardless of diagnosis
  • Use additional precautions (contact, droplet, airborne) as needed
  • Dispose of gloves and PPE properly in designated bins
  • Perform hand hygiene even when gloves are worn

📊 Key Statistic

Proper hand hygiene reduces healthcare-associated infections by up to 50% (CDC). Pain assessment tools are commonly overlooked as fomites — disinfect between patients!

🛡️ Safety Precautions — Patient & Nurse

Patient Safety

  • Verify patient identity (2 identifiers: name + DOB)
  • Assess mental status before asking pain questions
  • Position the patient comfortably during assessment
  • Ensure the call bell is within reach after assessment
  • Avoid causing additional pain during examination
  • Support painful areas during patient movement
  • Monitor for adverse effects of analgesics (respiratory depression, sedation)
  • Check for allergies before medication administration
  • Follow the "Rights of Medication Administration"
  • Watch for signs of medication interactions

Nurse Safety

  • Use PPE for suspected infectious patients
  • Practice safe body mechanics when moving patients
  • Ensure adequate assistance for repositioning
  • Report needle-stick injuries immediately
  • Be aware of workplace violence risks with agitated patients

🚫 The #1 Mistake

Doubting the patient's self-report is the most dangerous mistake. Evidence suggests a provider's observational pain report cannot be assumed to be an accurate indicator of the patient's pain (Powell et al.). Trust the patient!

🚩 Red Flags in Pain Assessment (Urgent)

  • Sudden severe pain (10/10) in a previously stable patient — possible acute event (MI, dissection, perforation)
  • Pain unrelieved by usual doses of prescribed analgesics — possible undertreatment or new pathology
  • Chest pain radiating to jaw/arm with diaphoresis and nausea — suspect MI
  • Sudden severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen — suspect perforation or peritonitis
  • Severe headache described as "the worst of my life" — suspect subarachnoid hemorrhage
  • Back pain with neurological signs (numbness, weakness, incontinence) — cauda equina
  • Pain with fever above 39°C — suspect infection/sepsis
  • Pain with respiratory distress or altered mental status
  • Signs of opioid overdose: RR less than 10/min, pinpoint pupils, decreased LOC
  • Pain during pregnancy with bleeding — obstetric emergency

🌳 Pain Assessment Decision Tree

Patient reports pain → assessed with the appropriate tool (NRS/VAS/FLACC/CPOT) → the decision is guided by the score:

0–3 Mild

Continue current care, non-pharm options, reassess q4h

4–6 Moderate

Change analgesic, give PRN dose, reassess in 15–30 min

7–10 Severe

Pain emergency — notify physician, IV analgesic ASAP, reassess in 15 min

  • BP above 140 mmHg systolic (hypertension)
  • RR above 20 breaths/min (tachypnea)
  • Pallor and diaphoresis
  • Pupil dilation
  • Nausea & vomiting

A stepwise approach to pain management based on severity, moving from non-opioids to weak opioids to strong opioids, with adjuvants added at any step.

Opioid Adverse Effects & Nursing Considerations

⚠️ Common Opioid Adverse Effects:

  • Respiratory depression (RR < 10)
  • Sedation and confusion
  • Constipation (very common)
  • Nausea and vomiting, pruritus, urinary retention
  • Miosis (pinpoint pupils)
  • Tolerance and dependence

🚨 Opioid Overdose — Emergency Triad:

  • Respiratory depression (RR < 10)
  • Pinpoint pupils (miosis)
  • Decreased level of consciousness (unresponsive)

Antidote: Naloxone (Narcan) 0.4–2mg IV/IM/SC, may repeat every 2–3 minutes.

✅ Nursing Considerations:

  • Check RR and sedation level before EACH opioid dose
  • Hold the dose if RR < 10 or excessive sedation
  • Give a stool softener alongside opioids
  • Assess allergies (especially morphine, codeine)
  • Never crush extended-release tablets
  • Educate the patient about safe use

🧒 Pediatric Pain Assessment — The QUESTT Approach

Does pain assessment differ with children? YES. Despite the outdated belief that children do not feel pain due to an underdeveloped nervous system, children DO experience pain — expressing and detecting it is simply more challenging than in adults. The QUESTT approach (Baker & Wong, 1987) was developed specifically for pediatric assessment.

LetterMeaning
QQuestion the child if verbal, and the parent/guardian for both verbal and non-verbal children
UUse pain rating scales if appropriate
EEvaluate behavior and physiological changes
SSecure the parent's involvement
TTake the cause of pain into account
TTake action and evaluate results

🎯 Key Principle: An effective pain assessment process is as important for children as for adults. Behavior alone is not always a reliable indicator — combine a pain scale WITH physiological indicators (BP, HR, RR).

FLACC Behavioral Pain Scale (Merkel et al., 1997)

Used for patients who cannot verbally report pain. Five categories — Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability — each scored 0–2, for a total of 0–10.

Category012
FaceNo expression, smileOccasional grimace, withdrawnFrequent/constant frown, clenched jaw
LegsNormal position, relaxedUneasy, restless, tenseKicking, or legs drawn up
ActivityLying quietly, moves easilySquirming, tenseArched, rigid, or jerking
CryNo cryMoans, whimpers, occasional complaintCrying steadily, screams, sobs
ConsolabilityContent, relaxedReassured by touch, hug, distractionDifficult to console/comfort

📊 Score Interpretation: 0 = relaxed and comfortable · 1–3 = mild discomfort · 4–6 = moderate pain · 7–10 = severe discomfort/pain. Observe an awake patient for 2–5 minutes with legs/body uncovered; observe a sleeping patient for at least 5 minutes.

Source: Merkel et al. (1997); Powell et al. (IASP).

Additional Pediatric Tools: TVP Scale & Pain Thermometer

Touch Visual Pain (TVP) Scale — for children unable or unwilling to report pain. A 10-point scale using touch and observation to assess pain and anxiety, based on signs such as asymmetrical head, verbalizations of pain, facial tension, clenched hands, crossed legs, shallow breathing, and increased/irregular heartbeat. Score 1 (present) or 0 (not present) per item for a baseline, give medication if needed, and reassess after 20–30 minutes.

Pain Thermometer (for children 7+) — an adaptation of the VDS that aligns a thermometer against words describing pain intensity. Useful for patients with cognitive deficits or communication difficulty; the Iowa Pain Thermometer version can also be used with younger children. Patients imagine that as the temperature rises, pain also increases, and mark the level accordingly.

Source: Powell et al. (IASP) — TVP is used in low-resource settings and requires further validation.

👶 Age-Specific Challenges in Pain Assessment

Neonates (0–1 month) — Behavioral observation only: This is the only way to assess pain. Involve family/guardian, who can advise on "normal" vs. "abnormal" behavior. Behavior is NOT necessarily an accurate indicator — absence of crying/movement does not always mean absence of pain. Follow national ethical guidelines for parent/guardian presence and consent.

Infants (1 month – 1 year) — Body signals: Body rigidity or thrashing; facial expression with brows lowered, eyes tightly closed, mouth open and squarish; intense or loud, inconsolable crying; drawing knees to chest; hypersensitivity/irritability; poor oral intake; unable to sleep.

Toddlers (1–2 years) — Verbal aggression: Verbally aggressive, cry intensely; regressive behavior, withdrawal; physical resistance, guarding of the painful area; unable to sleep. May be unable to communicate verbally, but behavior expresses their emotional and physical state — use play and drawings for non-verbal expression.

Preschoolers (3–5 years) — Pain as punishment: Can verbalize pain intensity but may see pain as punishment; thrash arms/legs, push stimuli away; uncooperative, may need physical restraint; cling to parent, request hugs/kisses. They need to trust the healthcare provider — take extra time, use open-ended questions.

School-aged (6–12 years) — Fear of consequences: Verbalize pain and can use objective measures, but may deny pain fearing consequences (exam, injection); influenced by cultural beliefs; pain-related nightmares; stalling behaviors; muscular rigidity. Involve them in their own care and give choices when possible.

Adolescents (13–18 years) — Peer influence: Verbalize pain but may deny it in front of peers; changes in sleep/appetite; muscle tension, regressive behavior with family. Show genuine interest, avoid confrontation, and focus on the adolescent as a person — not just the problem.

Source: Powell et al. (IASP), Chapter 10.

👴 Elderly & Dementia Considerations

Aged patients present additional challenges: visual or cognitive impairment; hearing impairment; social norms that discourage them from appearing as a burden; multiple morbidities and medications, especially problematic with dementia; frequent inadequate analgesia because they cannot communicate their need.

Principal rule for geriatric patients: ASK for pain — do not wait for a spontaneous complaint.

Strategies for Cognitively Intact Elderly:

  • Increase text size for visually impaired patients
  • Include relatives in the assessment when appropriate
  • Avoid "mental overload" (multiple topics, insufficient explanation)
  • Speak slowly and clearly, allow more time for responses
  • Use hearing aids if available

🚨 Non-Communicative Patients (Dementia): Assessment relies primarily on behavioral proxies — facial impression, daily activity, emotional reactions, response to consolation, and vegetative reactions — rather than any scale requiring communication. Use the PAINAD Scale.

Source: Powell et al. (IASP), Chapter 27 — Pain in Old Age and Dementia.

🤰 Pregnancy Considerations

Pain Assessment During Pregnancy:

  • Use the same pain scales (NRS, VAS, VDS) as for non-pregnant adults
  • Never dismiss pain as "normal pregnancy discomfort" without assessment
  • Distinguish physiological pregnancy pain from pathological pain
  • Consider trimester-specific pain patterns
  • Assess for obstetric emergencies: severe abdominal pain + bleeding = urgent
  • Monitor for preeclampsia: severe headache, epigastric pain, visual changes

Common pregnancy pain types: round ligament pain (2nd trimester), back pain, pelvic pain, Braxton-Hicks contractions, labor contractions.

🚨 Obstetric Red Flags — Requires Immediate Evaluation:

  • Severe abdominal pain + bleeding → abruption/miscarriage
  • Severe headache + visual changes → preeclampsia
  • Epigastric pain → HELLP syndrome
  • Regular contractions before 37 weeks → preterm labor
  • Sudden severe pain + shock → ectopic pregnancy rupture

🏥 ICU Considerations — CPOT & BPS

ICU Pain Assessment Challenges: Patients are often intubated/mechanically ventilated and cannot self-report; sedated patients require behavioral scales; multiple invasive procedures cause continuous pain. PADIS Guidelines (2018) recommend CPOT as the preferred tool for non-verbal ICU patients. Assess pain continuously, not just at intervals, and consider it BEFORE painful procedures (suctioning, positioning).

📋 Clinical Case Studies

Case 1 — Pediatric Pain Assessment: A 7-year-old girl with AIDS, not on antiretroviral therapy, is brought to a small rural hospital by her 13-year-old brother, appearing to be in some pain.

Answer:

  • The priority is to control the patient's pain as quickly as possible
  • At 7 years old, she should be able to verbalize her pain
  • Combine the body diagram and the Wong-Baker FACES scale to assess location, radiation, and severity
  • Full assessment may be delayed until pain is managed, depending on severity
  • Involve both the girl and her older brother, with her agreement
  • Explore brief family history to determine if an adult carer is available
  • Ensure appropriate consent is obtained before therapeutic interventions
  • If an adult carer cannot be located quickly, it may be necessary to assess and treat pain while waiting

Source: Powell et al. (IASP), Chapter 10 — Case Studies.

Case 2 — Elderly Non-Verbal Patient: A home-based care team finds an elderly woman with end-stage cancer curled up on her bed, crying, periodically drifting into a semi-conscious state.

Answer:

  • Presenting behavior (crying, fetal position) suggests pain
  • She is unable to respond verbally to a pain chart/scale
  • Take history from her carer: what worsens/relieves pain, duration, localized vs. referred
  • Use an observational tool such as PAINAD
  • In moments of consciousness, ask closed questions with squeeze/nod responses
  • Supplement with a quick physical examination
  • Base the assessment on observation + physical exam + simple questions + comprehensive carer history

Case 3 — Neonate with Suspected Pain: A week-old baby boy is brought in with projectile vomiting (suggestive of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, 1 in 500 babies) and will need surgery. He appears tense and agitated.

Answer: Use the FLACC scale (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability). Speak with his mother about duration, other symptoms, medical history, and aggravating/relieving factors. The underlying cause may be treatable with surgery — managing pain quickly also allows relaxation, making it easier to determine the cause.

Source: Powell et al. (IASP), Chapter 10 — Case Studies.

🚨 Rapid Pain Assessment in Emergencies

Rapid Pain Assessment Protocol (Emergency Department):

  1. Primary survey first — ABCDE before detailed pain assessment
  2. Quick screen — "On a scale of 0-10, how bad is your pain right now?"
  3. Location — "Point to where it hurts"
  4. Onset — "When did it start? What were you doing?"
  5. Character — "Describe it in one word"
  6. Immediate action if score ≥7 — IV access, notify the physician
  7. Full PQRSTU after stabilization

Emergency pain patterns to recognize:

  • MI: Crushing chest pain, radiates to jaw/arm
  • Aortic dissection: Tearing back pain
  • Perforation: Sudden severe abdominal pain
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage: "Thunderclap" headache
  • Ectopic pregnancy: Unilateral pelvic pain + shock
  • Kidney stone: Colicky flank pain
  • Testicular torsion: Sudden scrotal pain

Golden rules: (1) Never delay analgesia for diagnosis; (2) use the IV route for rapid onset (15-min peak); (3) reassess in 15 minutes; (4) document time, dose, and response; (5) watch for adverse effects.

💎 Clinical Pearls & Wisdom

  • Pain is subjective — accept the patient as the expert on their own body
  • Every question provides essential information about etiology and first steps to treatment
  • Pain intensity guides therapy: 0-3 no change; 4-7 change analgesic; 8-10 emergency
  • Pain quality differentiates etiology: "burning" → neuropathic; "dull, aching" → nociceptive; "unbearable" → affective valuation
  • Pain pattern of increase helps identify etiology: worst in early morning → inflammation; constant high level → chronic pain
  • Pain pattern of decrease is diagnostic: only rest helps → chronic pain; movement helps → possible osteoarthritis
  • Localization is probably the single most important question — it differentiates radicular from non-radicular pain
  • Age matters — pediatric pain requires the QUESTT approach; elderly patients require asking, not waiting
  • Behavior alone is unreliable — combine it with physiological indicators (BP, HR, RR)
  • Non-pharmacological interventions (Gate Control Theory) enhance pharmacological analgesia

Source: Powell et al., Guide to Pain Management in Low-Resource Settings, Chapter 10 (IASP) — Pearls of Wisdom.

⚡ Quick Revision

Key definitions: Pain (IASP 2020) — an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience with actual or potential tissue damage. Gate Control Theory (Melzack & Wall, 1965) — non-painful stimuli close the gate. Pain is the 5th vital sign (Joint Commission). Gold standard — the patient's self-report (McCaffery, 1968).

ScoreLevelAction
0NoneContinue monitoring
1-3MildNon-pharmacological, reassess q4h
4-6ModerateChange analgesic, reassess in 15-30 min
7-10SeverePain emergency, IV analgesic

Pain tools quick match: Conscious adults → NRS (0-10) · Children 3-8 yr → Wong-Baker FACES · <3 yr / non-verbal → FLACC (0-10) · ICU intubated → CPOT (0-8, gold standard) · Sedated → BPS (3-12) · Dementia → PAINAD (0-10) · Palliative care → APCA POS (0-5).

Reassessment timing: Oral analgesic → 30 min · IV analgesic → 15 min · Minimum in hospital → q4h · Always document the response after any intervention.

📝 Cheat Sheet

ComponentQuick reference
PQRSTUP=Provocative/Palliative • Q=Quality • R=Region/Radiation • S=Severity • T=Time • U=Understanding
OPQRSTO=Onset • P=Provocation • Q=Quality • R=Radiation • S=Severity • T=Time
OLDCARTSO=Onset • L=Location • D=Duration • C=Character • A=Aggravating • R=Relieving • T=Timing • S=Severity
QUESTT (peds)Q=Question • U=Use scales • E=Evaluate behavior • S=Secure parent • T=Take cause • T=Take action
FLACCFace • Legs • Activity • Cry • Consolability (each 0-2, total 0-10)
Pain scores0=None • 1-3=Mild • 4-6=Moderate • 7-10=Severe (emergency at 8-10)
WHO ladderStep 1: non-opioid → Step 2: weak opioid → Step 3: strong opioid (± adjuvants at each step)
Reassessment15 min post-IV • 30 min post-oral • q4h routine minimum
Opioid overdose triadRR <10 + pinpoint pupils + decreased LOC → naloxone 0.4-2 mg IV
Physiological signs↑HR, ↑BP, ↑RR, pallor, diaphoresis, pupil dilation (sympathetic activation)
Behavioral signsGrimacing, guarding, moaning, restlessness, clenched fists, withdrawal
Pain typesAcute (<30d) • Chronic (>3-6mo) • Nociceptive (tissue) • Neuropathic (nerve) • Referred • Phantom

Non-pharmacological interventions (Gate Control): massage, heat/cold, TENS, distraction (music, TV), guided imagery, deep breathing, repositioning, cutaneous stimulation.

✅ OSCE Checklist — Pain Assessment (20 points)

  1. Introduction: greet the patient, introduce yourself, verify identity (2 identifiers)
  2. Consent: explain the procedure, obtain verbal consent
  3. Hand hygiene: wash hands / use alcohol-based rub
  4. Privacy: provide a privacy screen if needed
  5. Position: ensure patient comfort and good lighting
  6. P — Provocation: "What makes it better/worse?"
  7. Q — Quality: "How does it feel? Sharp/dull/burning?"
  8. R — Region/Radiation: "Show me where. Does it spread?"
  9. S — Severity: use an appropriate scale (NRS/VAS/FACES)
  10. T — Time: "Continuous or intermittent? How long?"
  11. U — Understanding: "How is it affecting your life?"
  12. Home remedies: ask about non-pharmacological and pharmacological measures used
  13. Behavioral observation: facial expression, guarding, body position
  14. Physiological signs: HR, BP, RR, diaphoresis, pallor
  15. Documentation: complete the pain assessment form
  16. Plan interventions: pharmacological + non-pharmacological
  17. Patient education: explain the pain management plan
  18. Reassessment plan: state when to reassess (15/30 min)
  19. Hand hygiene: wash hands after patient contact
  20. Report: communicate findings to the physician if needed

👨‍⚖️ OSCE Examiner Tips

DO (high marks): start with a clear introduction and consent; maintain eye contact; use open-ended questions first; show empathy ("that sounds difficult"); use the patient's own words when documenting; believe the patient's self-report; ask about impact on function; verbalize your findings out loud; state the reassessment plan clearly; complete hand hygiene visibly.

DON'T (lose marks): skip introduction or consent; use jargon the patient won't understand; doubt or minimize the patient's pain; estimate pain visually without a scale; rush through PQRSTU; forget non-verbal observation; skip hand hygiene; focus only on the numeric score; ignore cultural factors; fail to document reassessment.

Communication phrases that earn marks: "I understand you're in pain — let me help you." · "On a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 is no pain and 10 is the worst pain you can imagine, what number would you give your pain right now?" · "Can you describe the pain in your own words?" · "Is there anything that makes it better or worse?" · "How is this pain affecting your daily activities?" · "I'll come back in 30 minutes to check on you."

Time management: a typical OSCE station is 7-10 minutes. Allocate roughly: 1 min intro + consent, 4-5 min PQRSTU assessment, 1 min observation, 1-2 min documentation/plan, 1 min conclusion + reassessment plan.

🧠 Memory Tricks & Mnemonics

PQRSTU — "People Question Real Suffering Truly Understand": People→Provocative/Palliative, Question→Quality, Real→Region/Radiation, Suffering→Severity, Truly→Time, Understand→Understanding/Impact.

FLACC — "Face Legs Activity Cry Consolability": think of a baby — watch their Face, look at their Legs, note their Activity, listen to their Cry, try to Console them.

QUESTT (pediatric) — Question the child (if verbal) and parent (always); Use appropriate scales; Evaluate behavior + physiological changes; Secure parent's involvement; Take cause into account; Take action + evaluate results.

Opioid overdose — "Triple P": Pinpoint pupils (miosis), Poor breathing (RR <10), Poor consciousness (decreased LOC). Treatment: naloxone (Narcan) 0.4-2 mg IV/IM.

Pain types: Acute (sudden, <30 days) · Chronic (>3-6 months) · Nociceptive (tissue damage) · Somatic (skin/bone/muscle) · Visceral (organs) · Neuropathic (burning/shooting) · Referred (distant site, e.g. MI → jaw) · Phantom (amputated limb).

🗂️ AI Flashcards

Q: Define pain per IASP (2020)? A: Unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage.
Q: Four stages of the pain pathway? A: Transduction → Transmission → Perception → Modulation.
Q: Best tool for an intubated ICU patient? A: CPOT (0-8); score >2 = significant pain.
Q: FLACC categories? A: Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (0-2 each, total 0-10).
Q: When to reassess after an IV analgesic? A: 15 minutes (peak effect).
Q: When to reassess after an oral analgesic? A: 30 minutes (peak effect).
Q: WHO Analgesic Ladder Step 1? A: Non-opioid (paracetamol, NSAIDs) ± adjuvants.
Q: WHO Analgesic Ladder Step 3? A: Strong opioid (morphine, fentanyl) + non-opioid ± adjuvants.
Q: Opioid overdose triad? A: RR <10, pinpoint pupils, decreased LOC. Antidote: naloxone.
Q: QUESTT stands for? A: Question, Use scales, Evaluate, Secure parent, Take cause, Take action.
Q: Gate Control Theory — year and authors? A: 1965, Melzack & Wall.
Q: Best scale for a dementia patient? A: PAINAD (0-10) — observational tool.

📚 AI Revision Notes — Top 20 for Exams

  1. IASP definition: unpleasant sensory + emotional experience with tissue damage
  2. Pain = 5th vital sign (Joint Commission)
  3. Gold standard: the patient's self-report
  4. Pain pathway: transduction → transmission → perception → modulation
  5. Gate Control Theory: Melzack & Wall (1965)
  6. Adult scale: NRS (0-10), most common
  7. Pediatric <3 yr: FLACC
  8. Pediatric 3-8 yr: Wong-Baker FACES
  9. ICU intubated: CPOT (gold standard)
  10. Dementia: PAINAD
  11. Score interpretation: 0-3 mild, 4-6 moderate, 7-10 severe (8-10 emergency)
  12. Reassess: 15 min post-IV, 30 min post-oral
  13. WHO ladder: non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid
  14. PQRSTU: Provocative-Quality-Region-Severity-Time-Understanding
  15. QUESTT: Question-Use-Evaluate-Secure-Take-Take (pediatric)
  16. Neuropathic pain: burning, shooting, electrical
  17. Nociceptive pain: dull, aching
  18. Opioid overdose: RR<10 + pinpoint pupils + ↓LOC → naloxone
  19. Referred pain: chest pain → jaw (MI); shoulder pain (diaphragm)
  20. Phantom pain: real pain in an amputated limb

Most tested concepts in NCLEX/Prometric: patient's self-report is the gold standard; reassessment timing (15/30 min); selecting the correct scale for age/condition; WHO analgesic ladder steps; opioid safety and overdose management; non-pharmacological interventions (Gate Control).

🎓 Licensing Exam Tips (NCLEX/Prometric)

Pain assessment priorities: always believe the patient — self-report is the gold standard; assess before you intervene; prioritize physiological needs (Maslow) — pain affects safety and the ABCs; try non-pharmacological measures first for mild pain (Gate Control support); a combined pharmacological + non-pharmacological approach gives the best results; reassess after every intervention — critical for passing; never delegate pain assessment to unlicensed staff — it requires nursing judgment; respect cultural differences in pain expression.

Prometric exam focus (Egypt/Gulf): WHO Analgesic Ladder application, correct scale for the patient population, documentation standards, pediatric pain (FLACC, Wong-Baker), post-operative pain management, cultural/religious considerations.

Common trap questions: the question asks for the "PRIORITY" — safety first, then pain; don't assume vital signs alone confirm pain accuracy (false); watch for the wrong scale for the patient's age; don't give an analgesic without stating a reassessment plan; never dismiss the patient's self-report.

Test-taking strategy: read the stem carefully — identify age, setting, condition; look for keywords ("priority", "first action", "most appropriate"); apply Maslow — physiological before psychological; apply ABC — airway, breathing, circulation before pain; choose assessment before intervention unless it's an emergency; choose the patient's report over the nurse's observation; choose a systematic approach (PQRSTU) over random questions.

❓ Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What if a patient doesn't want to rate their pain? Respect their choice and use behavioral observation instead. Document "patient declined to rate" and describe the observed signs (grimacing, guarding, vital sign changes).

Q: How often should I reassess pain? Minimum every 4 hours in hospital; 15 minutes after IV analgesic; 30 minutes after oral; after any procedure; whenever the patient complains.

Q: What if the patient scores 10/10 but appears comfortable? Believe the patient — pain is subjective, and cultural and psychological factors affect its expression. Never say "you don't look like you're in pain."

Q: Can I estimate pain visually without a scale? No — always use validated scales. A nurse's visual estimation is unreliable per research (Powell et al.).

Q: Which scale for a patient who speaks a different language? Wong-Baker FACES (no language needed) or a translated NRS. A body diagram helps with location.

Q: When should I call the physician about pain? Score 7-10, sudden severe onset, unresponsive to analgesic, new radiating pain, or associated red flags (chest pain, dyspnea, altered LOC).

Q: What is the maximum daily paracetamol dose? Adults: 4 g/day (4000 mg). Elderly or liver disease: 2-3 g/day — always check.

Q: How do I assess pain in a comatose patient? Use behavioral scales — CPOT (if in ICU), FLACC, or PAINAD — and watch for grimacing, guarding, HR/BP/RR changes, and restlessness.

Q: Can I give more analgesic if the score is still high after reassessment? Follow the physician's order. If pain persists above 4 despite the maximum dose, contact the physician for new orders and consider a multimodal approach.

🧠 Test Yourself — Multiple Choice

[[MCQ_QUIZ]]

✅ Test Yourself — True or False

Tap "True" or "False" — the explanation appears immediately.

[[TF_QUIZ]]

📝 Fill in the Blank

[[FB_QUIZ]]

🌟 Key Takeaways

  1. Believe the patient — their self-report is the gold standard
  2. Pain is the 5th vital sign — assess it systematically
  3. Use validated scales for the appropriate population
  4. Reassess after every intervention (15 or 30 min)
  5. Multimodal analgesia works best
  6. Non-pharmacological interventions support pharmacological ones (Gate Control)
  7. Consider special populations: children, elderly, ICU, pregnancy
  8. Document accurately using the patient's own words
  9. Recognize red flags requiring urgent intervention
  10. Advocate for adequate pain management — it is a patient right

Final message from the author: Pain assessment is not just a task — it's an act of compassion. Every time you take the time to properly assess a patient's pain, you're validating their experience and giving them the care they deserve. Never dismiss, never doubt. Just listen, observe, document, and act.

⚖️ Pain Assessment Tools — Advantages & Disadvantages

ToolAdvantagesDisadvantages
VASQuick, simple, well validated, easily translated, sensitive to changeToo abstract for some; problematic with cognitive/visual/physical disability
NRSQuick, simple, usable verbally, well validated, easy to teach, detects treatment effectsDecreased reliability at age extremes; unreliable for non-verbal/cognitively impaired patients
VDSQuick, easily comprehended, well validated, intuitively preferredLanguage-dependent; cultural interpretation issues; problematic for very young/old/illiterate patients
Wong-Baker FACESSimple, quick, no reading required, unaffected by gender/ethnicitySometimes described as measuring mood rather than pain; crying faces not culturally universal
FLACCUseful for non-verbal children; quick, easily reproducibleNot validated for special-needs children, neonates, or ventilated children
TVPUseful for children unable to report; quick, easily reproducibleRequires further validation research across different populations
Pain thermometerSimple, quick, intuitive for those uncomfortable with numbersProblematic for cognitively/visually impaired patients
CPOTGold standard for ICU; high sensitivity/specificity; validated for non-verbal patientsRequires a trained observer; not usable with complete paralysis
PAINADUseful for advanced dementia; quick, easily reproducibleRelies on proxy indicators; less specific than self-report
APCA POSComprehensive palliative care assessment; WHO-endorsedAddresses pain as only one domain; requires staff training

Source: Powell et al. (IASP), Appendix 2 — McLafferty and Farley (2008).
