title_en: IV Cannula Insertion — Illustrated Steps
excerpt_en: An illustrated 15-step guide to peripheral IV cannula insertion: equipment, gauges and colors, vein selection, tips, complications and dwell time.
content_en:
📚 For deeper theory: this article is an illustrated step-by-step guide to IV cannula insertion. For anatomy, aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT), complications, special populations, documentation and assessment questions, see the Comprehensive Nursing Guide to IV Cannulation.

🎯 Overview

Definition

The IV cannula is a type of needle used to give the patient intravenous fluids (IV fluids), medications and blood products through a vein.

Most exposed persons: patients who are treated with intravenous injections.

🧰 Equipment Required

  • Tourniquet
  • Cannulas in different sizes
  • Medical cotton
  • Adhesive plaster strips
  • Gloves

Equipment photos

✅ Indications (Purpose of Use)

To give intravenous medications and fluids for the following reasons:

  • To treat the patient more quickly.
  • To replace fluid lost from the body.
  • To transfuse blood and other blood components.
  • To replace fluid loss in adults in dehydration and burns.
  • To give intravenous medications and fluids to adults, such as antibiotics.
  • Perfusion of the veins before surgery.
  • To raise blood pressure and restore the balance of salts and fluids in the body (fluid balance).

⛔ Contraindications

  • Infection
  • Inflammation of blood vessels
  • Burns
  • Injuries
  • Intravenous and arterial herniation

🩸 Difference Between Artery and Vein

FeatureArteryVein
CarriesOxygenated blood from the heart to the tissuesDeoxygenated blood from the tissues to the heart
WallsThickThin
LumenSmallLarge
ElasticityElasticLess elastic
ValvesNo valvesValves present to prevent backflow of blood
LocationDeep seated and cannot be seenLies closer to the skin and can be seen clearly
PulseA pulse is presentNo pulse
PressureHigh pressureLow pressure

📍 Most Common Cannulation Sites

  • Cephalic vein
  • Subclavian vein
  • Basilic vein
  • Median antebrachial vein
  • Radial vein
  • Metacarpal vein
  • Digital vein

🔧 Main Parts of the Cannula

No.PartFunction / Description
1NeedleThe metal needle of the cannula that enters the skin and vein
2CatheterThe plastic part that stays inside the vein
3WingsThe wings of the cannula
4Injection port capThe upper cap of the injection port
5Needle gripThe part used to pull out the needle of the cannula
6Flashback chamberThe part in which blood appears
7Lock plugThe valve that closes the cannula

💉 Types of Cannulas (Gauges and Colors)

GaugeColorExternal diameterLengthFlow rateUse
14GOrange2.1 mm45 mm240 ml/minTransfusing large amounts of blood and fluids very rapidly
16GGrey1.8 mm45 mm180 ml/minAlso inserted for blood transfusion and when a large amount of fluid is needed
18GGreen1.3 mm32/45 mm90 ml/minInserted for blood transfusion and when a large amount of fluid is needed
20GPink1.1 mm32 mm60 ml/minFor maintenance fluids and adults, and can be used for blood transfusion
22GBlue0.9 mm25 mm36 ml/minFor older children
24GYellow0.7 mm19 mm20 ml/minFor children
26GViolet0.6 mm19 mm13 ml/minFor children with thin and small veins

Notes:

  • The higher the number, the smaller the cannula size (narrower and shorter). The lower the number, the larger the cannula size (wider and longer).
  • The numbers for flow rate and catheter length differ according to the manufacturer, but in the end they are all close to each other.

👀 Characteristics of a Suitable Vein

When preparing for cannulation, the vein should be:

  • Visible
  • Clear and palpable
  • Bouncy
  • Soft
  • Fixed, not movable, and well supported
  • Straight and non-tortuous

📋 Insertion Steps (15 Steps)

1. Verify the patient identity

Confirm the identity of the patient and check the full (four-part) name.

2. Wash hands and put on gloves

Wash your hands and put on gloves.

3. Tie the forearm with a tourniquet

Tie a tourniquet around the forearm, preferably the less-used forearm.

Make sure the tourniquet is placed correctly. Tying above the level of the vein prevents blood from returning from it to the heart, so it fills with blood and becomes more visible. Take care, however, that the tourniquet is not too tight so that it does not cut off the circulation completely.

Use the correct way to feel for the vein. Contrary to common belief, you should palpate the arm, not slap it, because slapping the arm is a poor method and may cause a hematoma under the skin. Use your index finger to find the location of the vein, and recognize it by its spongy softness. Do not use your thumb because you may feel your own pulse in it.

4. Reassure the patient

Ask the patient to relax. Many people have a phobia of needles, and their anxiety or apprehension about cannulation is a natural result of that. Calm the patient and explain that the pain is mild and momentary.

To make the vein more prominent, ask the patient to clench the fist and open it several times.

5. Avoid vein bifurcations

Avoid inserting the cannula at points where veins branch or join, because this increases the chance of bleeding under the skin.

6. Disinfect the insertion site

Disinfect the catheter insertion site with 70% alcohol (spirit) and leave it to dry. Do not touch the site after disinfection.

Remember: let the antiseptic (alcohol) dry before inserting the needle. Do not blow on it or fan it with your hand, so that the site does not become contaminated.

7. Anchor the vein

Anchor the vein by pulling the skin taut below the injection site, to stop the vein from rolling away. Be careful not to touch the area that has been disinfected.

8. Insert the needle

Insert the needle at an angle of 15–30 degrees and hold it steady in this position.

9. Watch for blood flashback

Watch for a flash of blood in its known place in the cannula (the flashback chamber) as a sign that the vein wall has been penetrated. Then continue advancing slowly while withdrawing the metal needle out of the vein.

Do not attempt the insertion again with the same cannula.

10. Press on the vein before withdrawing the needle

Before removing the metal needle, press on the vein above the cannula so that blood does not come out and bleeding does not occur.

11. Dispose of the cannula needle

Dispose of the cannula needle immediately after use in the safety box designated for sharps waste.

12. Release the tourniquet and test the cannula

Release the tourniquet from the forearm, then connect the IV set to the cannula to test that it works efficiently, or inject a small amount of distilled water into the cannula.

13. Secure the cannula

Secure the cannula with adhesive tape and write down the date of insertion.

14. Care of the insertion site

Leave the insertion site dry and visible.

15. Clean up and tidy

Clean the equipment used, return everything to its place and prepare it for the next use.

Practical training follows.

💡 Important Tips for IV Injection and Cannulation

Here are 5 basic tips for inserting a cannula easily.

1. Do not use only your eyes to look for the vein

Sometimes you cannot see the vein. If you rely only on seeing veins for IV injection or cannulation, you will of course miss many easy veins that you could use. Try to use your sense of touch while searching for the vein: touch some veins and notice the difference between them and the muscles and fat.

Try doing this with your eyes closed, as it will improve your ability to tell them apart, and it is a good way to train.

2. Pull the skin taut and steady

All veins are rounded (cylindrical), but some of them are not completely so, especially in older people with thin skin. In these cases pulling the skin taut is essential, because searching for and chasing veins is not the only thing that hurts the patient. There is also the risk of cutting and injuring the vein during the injection. So try to pull the skin steadily below and above the site you will inject, using your other hand.

3. Using or not using the tourniquet

Sometimes using the tourniquet is a bad idea. If the vein is clearly visible and you can easily identify it, it is better not to use the tourniquet. But if you do use it, be careful not to tie it too tightly so that it does not cause the vein to burst when the needle penetrates it.

If the vein bursts while the tourniquet is on, remove it quickly and try inserting the cannula in another place.

4. Use a needle of suitable size

Use a needle of suitable size according to the vein available to you and according to the intended use.

5. Do not let unsuccessful attempts affect you

All of us, without exception, miss veins, and even professionals miss them often. The reason may be either using a wrong technique or the vein being weak and not visible. Know well that no one succeeds in cannulation or IV injection 100% of the time.

So do not let a failed attempt frustrate you. Be confident in yourself and keep trying. The more you try, the more your skill grows time after time, and you will become proficient with time.

If the attempt fails again, stop trying after the second attempt and call a colleague who has experience in cannulation.

Some difficulties that may occur during cannulation: the elderly and children, trauma patients, patients with food poisoning and watery diarrhea, patients receiving chemotherapy, obese patients, bleeding cases, and very prominent veins because they move, which makes inserting the cannula into them difficult.

🩹 Removing the Cannula

Remember: when removing the cannula, you must press on the vein in front of the plastic part (catheter) that is inside the vein so that you do not get bleeding (hemorrhage). Then withdraw it gently, and then place a dry cotton ball.

⚠️ Possible Complications of the IV Cannula

ComplicationDescription
PhlebitisInflammation (irritation) of the vein
InfectionInfection at the cannula site
PetechiaeA small red or purple spot caused by bleeding in the skin
Hematoma (bruising)A blood swelling, which is a bruise
Air embolismBlockage of blood vessels caused by one or more air bubbles or other gases in the circulation

⏱️ How Long Can the Cannula Stay in the Vein?

The maximum duration for a cannula to stay in place should be 72 hours, but if you do not notice signs of thrombophlebitis, leave it in place.

What are the Signs of Thrombophlebitis?

This is inflammation in the vein. Its signs are that you will notice at the cannula site:

  • Redness
  • Swelling
  • Pain
  • Mild edema (the cannula has leaked under the skin)

So if you notice any sign of thrombophlebitis, even on the first day, remove the cannula from its place immediately.

The cannula can also be removed in the following two situations:

  • Immediately after a blood transfusion.
  • Or once it is no longer needed.

🔍 Spot the Mistake in These Two Pictures

Look carefully at both pictures and try to find the mistake in each before reviewing the steps and tips above.

📌 Quick Review

  • Purpose: to give fluids and medications and transfuse blood quickly through a vein.
  • Suitable vein: visible, palpable, bouncy, soft, fixed, straight.
  • The higher the gauge number (G), the smaller the cannula: 14G orange is the largest and 26G violet is the smallest.
  • Tourniquet above the injection site, and do not touch the disinfected area and let the 70% alcohol dry.
  • Insert at 15–30 degrees, then watch for blood flashback.
  • Press on the vein above the cannula before withdrawing the needle, then dispose of it in the safety box.
  • Secure the cannula and write the date, and leave the site dry and visible.
  • Maximum stay is 72 hours, and it is removed immediately at any sign of phlebitis.
  • After two failed attempts, call an experienced colleague.

title: العلامات الحيوية: الدليل الشامل للممرض
excerpt: دليل تمريضي شامل لقياس العلامات الحيوية الخمسة: الحرارة، النبض، التنفس، ضغط الدم، وتشبع الأكسجين — القيم الطبيعية، خطوات القياس، العلامات التحذيرية، وأدوات الإنذار المبكر NEWS2.
content:
🩺 مهارة تمريضية أساسية — مستوى الدليل: A (WHO / AHA / NICE / AACN / Potter & Perry)

⏱ وقت القراءة: 20–25 دقيقة · وقت الدراسة الكامل: ~ساعتين · المستوى: مبتدئ – متوسط

🎯 الأهداف التعليمية

بعد الانتهاء من هذا الدليل ستكون قادرًا على:

  • تعريف العلامات الحيوية وتحديد مكوناتها الخمسة الأساسية.

  • حفظ المعدلات الطبيعية لكل علامة حيوية في البالغين والأطفال.

  • فهم أهمية العلامات الحيوية في التقييم التمريضي.

  • التعرف على العوامل التي تؤثر على دقة القراءات.

  • التمييز بين القراءات الطبيعية وغير الطبيعية وتحديد Red Flags التي تستدعي تدخلًا فوريًا.

  • تطبيق خطوات القياس الصحيحة لكل علامة حيوية.

  • توثيق النتائج والإبلاغ عن أي قراءة غير طبيعية باستخدام SBAR.

  • استخدام NEWS2 وqSOFA وMEWS لتقييم تدهور المريض.

  • مراعاة الاعتبارات الخاصة بالأطفال وكبار السن والحوامل ومرضى ICU.

  • فهم تأثير بعض الأدوية على العلامات الحيوية.

📖 المقدمة

تُعد العلامات الحيوية (Vital Signs) من أهم المؤشرات التي يعتمد عليها الممرض لتقييم الحالة الصحية للمريض، لأنها تعكس الوظائف الأساسية للجسم وتساعد على اكتشاف أي تغيرات أو تدهور صحي في وقت مبكر.

سواء كنت تعمل في قسم الطوارئ، أو العناية المركزة، أو الأقسام الداخلية، أو العيادات الخارجية، فإن قياس العلامات الحيوية يعتبر أول خطوة في التقييم التمريضي (Nursing Assessment).

ولا يقتصر دور الممرض على قياس القيم فقط، بل يشمل أيضًا تفسير النتائج، ومقارنتها بالقراءات السابقة، والإبلاغ عن أي تغيرات غير طبيعية في الوقت المناسب، واستخدام أدوات التنبؤ المبكر كـ NEWS2 لتحديد المرضى المعرضين للتدهور.

📘 التعريف — ما هي العلامات الحيوية؟

العلامات الحيوية (Vital Signs) هي مجموعة من القياسات التي تعكس كفاءة عمل أجهزة الجسم الحيوية، وتُستخدم لمتابعة الحالة الصحية للمريض واكتشاف أي تغيرات قد تشير إلى وجود مشكلة صحية.

تشمل العلامات الحيوية الأساسية:

  1. 🌡️ درجة حرارة الجسم (Body Temperature)

  2. ❤️ النبض (Pulse)

  3. 🫁 معدل التنفس (Respiratory Rate)

  4. 🩸 ضغط الدم (Blood Pressure)

  5. 🫧 تشبع الأكسجين (Oxygen Saturation – SpO₂)

💡 في بعض المؤسسات الصحية يُعتبر الألم (Pain) العلامة الحيوية السادسة، لأنه يؤثر بشكل مباشر على تقييم المريض وخطة الرعاية.

💙 أهمية العلامات الحيوية للممرض

  • تقييم الحالة العامة للمريض.

  • الكشف المبكر عن التدهور السريري (Clinical Deterioration).

  • متابعة استجابة المريض للعلاج.

  • توفير بيانات مرجعية (Baseline) للمقارنة مع القياسات المستقبلية.

  • اكتشاف العدوى أو النزيف أو الصدمة في مراحل مبكرة.

  • اتخاذ القرار المناسب بشأن إبلاغ الطبيب أو الممرض المسؤول.

  • حساب نتائج Early Warning Scores لتوجيه مستوى الرعاية.

🫀 التشريح والفسيولوجيا

🧠 Hypothalamus — منطقة تحت المهاد: ينظم درجة حرارة الجسم ويحافظ عليها ضمن المعدل الطبيعي من خلال التحكم في إنتاج الحرارة وفقدانها.

❤️ Heart — القلب: يضخ الدم إلى جميع أجزاء الجسم، ويؤثر مباشرةً على النبض وضغط الدم.

🫁 Lungs — الرئتان: مسؤولتان عن تبادل الأكسجين وثاني أكسيد الكربون، وبذلك تؤثران على معدل التنفس وتشبع الأكسجين.

🩸 Blood Vessels — الأوعية الدموية: يتغير ضغط الدم تبعًا لاتساع أو انقباض الأوعية الدموية، إضافةً إلى حجم الدم الذي يضخه القلب.

📋 دواعي القياس

  • ✅ عند استقبال المريض لأول مرة (Admission Baseline).

  • ✅ قبل وبعد العمليات الجراحية.

  • ✅ قبل وبعد إعطاء بعض الأدوية (مثل مضادات الضغط، مدرات البول، Beta Blockers).

  • ✅ عند حدوث أي تغير مفاجئ في حالة المريض.

  • ✅ أثناء الحمى أو الاشتباه بالعدوى.

  • ✅ عند الشكوى من ألم شديد.

  • ✅ بشكل دوري للمرضى المنومين وفق بروتوكول القسم.

  • ✅ حسب أوامر الطبيب.

🚫 الموانع والاحتياطات

🌡️ قياس درجة الحرارة عن طريق الفم — لا يُستخدم إذا كان المريض:

  • فاقد الوعي

  • يتنفس بالأكسجين عالي التدفق

  • تناول مشروبات ساخنة أو باردة خلال آخر 20 دقيقة

  • أجرى جراحة في الفم أو الفك

🩸 قياس ضغط الدم — لا يُقاس في ذراع بها:

  • ❌ وصلة غسيل كلوي (AV Fistula)

  • ❌ قسطرة وريدية نشطة

  • ❌ وذمة شديدة

  • ❌ جرح أو حرق

  • ❌ نفس الجهة التي أُجري فيها استئصال الثدي (Mastectomy)

🔬 خطوات القياس

🌡️ أولاً: قياس درجة الحرارة (Body Temperature)

الخطوات: اغسل يديك، تأكد من نوع جهاز الحرارة وصلاحيته، ثم اختر موضع القياس المناسب:

الموضعRouteالقيمة الطبيعيةملاحظة
الفمOral36.5–37.5°Cالمرجع الأساسي — انتظر 20 دقيقة بعد المشروبات
الإبطAxillary36.0–37.0°Cأقل بـ ~0.5°C من الفموية
الأذنTympanic36.5–37.5°Cسريع وعملي — تأكد من وضع الجهاز بشكل صحيح
الجبهةTemporal36.5–37.5°Cمناسب للأطفال وسريع

⚠️ تختلف قيم الحرارة الطبيعية حسب طريقة القياس، لذا يجب دائمًا ذكر موضع القياس عند التوثيق لتجنب التفسير الخاطئ للنتائج.

بعد اختيار الموضع: ضع الجهاز بالطريقة الصحيحة، انتظر حتى انتهاء القياس واسمع صوت التنبيه، ثم اقرأ النتيجة وسجّلها فورًا مع ذكر موضع القياس.

❤️ ثانياً: قياس النبض (Pulse Assessment)

الموضع الأكثر استخدامًا: ✅ Radial Artery (الشريان الكعبري).

  1. اطلب من المريض إراحة ذراعه على سطح مستوٍ.

  2. ضع إصبعَي السبابة والوسطى على الشريان الكعبري. ❌ لا تستخدم الإبهام (يحتوي على نبضه الخاص).

  3. عد النبض: 30 ثانية × 2 إذا كان منتظمًا، أو 60 ثانية كاملة إذا كان غير منتظم.

  4. قيّم ثلاثة عناصر: Rate (المعدل)، Rhythm (الإيقاع: منتظم/غير منتظم)، Strength (القوة: قوي/ضعيف/خيطي).

  5. سجّل النتائج.

🩺 إذا كان النبض غير منتظم، انتقل إلى قياس Apical Pulse لمدة دقيقة كاملة وأبلغ المسؤول.

🫁 ثالثاً: قياس معدل التنفس (Respiratory Rate)

  1. بعد الانتهاء من قياس النبض، استمر في وضع يدك على معصم المريض حتى لا ينتبه.

  2. راقب حركة الصدر صعودًا وهبوطًا.

  3. عُدّ كل شهيق + زفير = نفس واحد.

  4. احسب لمدة 30 ثانية × 2 إذا كان منتظمًا، أو 60 ثانية إذا كان غير منتظم.

  5. قيّم أربعة عناصر: Rate، Rhythm، Depth (العمق: سطحي/طبيعي/عميق)، Effort (الجهد: سهل أم يتطلب مجهودًا).

🩸 رابعاً: قياس ضغط الدم (Blood Pressure)

  1. أرح المريض لمدة 5 دقائق قبل القياس.

  2. اجعل الذراع في مستوى القلب.

  3. اختر حجم الكُف المناسب (يغطي 80% من محيط العضد).

  4. لُف الكُف على بُعد 2–3 سم فوق الحفرة المرفقية.

  5. ضع السماعة فوق الشريان العضدي (Brachial Artery).

  6. انفخ الكُف حتى يختفي النبض ثم أضف 20–30 mmHg إضافية.

  7. فرّغ الهواء بمعدل 2–3 mmHg في الثانية.

  8. سجّل: Systolic (أول صوت كورتكوف)، Diastolic (اختفاء الصوت)، الذراع المستخدمة، ووضعية المريض.

⚠️ لا يُشخَّص ارتفاع ضغط الدم أو انخفاضه بناءً على قراءة واحدة. يجب دائمًا تفسير القراءة في ضوء السياق السريري الكامل وإرشادات المنشأة، ومقارنتها بالـ Baseline.

🫧 خامساً: قياس تشبع الأكسجين (SpO₂)

  1. تأكد من أن إصبع المريض نظيف ودافئ.

  2. أزل طلاء الأظافر إذا أمكن.

  3. ضع جهاز Pulse Oximeter على الإصبع.

  4. انتظر حتى تثبت القراءة (10–15 ثانية).

  5. سجّل: SpO₂، Pulse Rate، ونوع التنفس (Room Air / O₂ / Ventilator).

⚠️ < 95%: يستدعي المتابعة والتقييم السريري.

⚠️ < 92%: يحتاج تقييمًا سريعًا في معظم البالغين.

🚨 < 90%: Red Flag يدل على نقص أكسجة شديد ويستلزم تدخلًا عاجلًا.

في بعض المرضى (مثل مرضى COPD)، قد تكون القيم الطبيعية لديهم أقل — راجع دائمًا Baseline المريض وتعليمات الطبيب.

💡 نصائح تمريضية عملية

💡 قارن دائمًا القراءة الحالية بـ Baseline المريض وليس بالقيم الطبيعية العامة فقط.

💡 سجّل وضعية المريض وموضع قياس الحرارة أثناء التوثيق لأنهما يؤثران على القراءة.

💡 إذا اختلفت قراءة SpO₂ عن الحالة السريرية، تحقق من دفء الإصبع وغياب طلاء الأظافر.

💡 في المرضى المسنين، انتبه لـ Orthostatic Hypotension — قس الضغط جالسًا ثم واقفًا.

💡 التنفس هو العلامة الأولى التي تتغير عند تدهور المريض — لا تهملها أبدًا.

💡 لا تقس الحرارة فورًا بعد الاستحمام أو ممارسة النشاط البدني — انتظر 20–30 دقيقة.

💡 مريض يأخذ Beta Blockers قد يكون HR = 55 bpm طبيعيًا له — تحقق من الأدوية قبل تصنيف القراءة.

🌡️ درجة الحرارة: لا تستخدم ميزان حرارة زئبقي مع طفل أو مريض فاقد الوعي. تجنب القياس الفموي إذا كان المريض غير متعاون.

🩸 ضغط الدم: لا تقس في ذراع بها AV Fistula أو بعد Mastectomy أو بها إصابة شديدة.

❤️ النبض: إذا تعذّر جس النبض الكعبري، انتقل إلى موضع آخر مناسب (Carotid, Femoral, Apical).

🫧 Pulse Oximeter: لا تعتمد على قراءة الجهاز وحدها إذا كانت لا تتوافق مع الحالة السريرية للمريض. برودة الأطراف أو ضعف الدورة الدموية يُقلّلان من دقة القراءة.

🔀 شجرات القرار (Decision Trees)

🌲 انخفاض ضغط الدم (SBP < 90 mmHg)

SBP < 90؟ → أعد القياس للتأكد → لا يزال < 90؟
  نعم → أضجع المريض وارفع قدميه → قيّم ABCDE (الوعي/لون الجلد/الأعراض)
        → أبلغ الطبيب فورًا بـ SBAR → ابدأ IV Access وتابع كل 5 دقائق
  لا  → راقب المريض وسجّل القراءة

🌲 انخفاض SpO₂ (< 95%)

تأكد من الجهاز أولًا (الإصبع دافئ؟ لا يوجد طلاء أظافر؟ الجهاز ثابت؟)
  القراءة موثوقة → هل < 92%؟
     نعم → هل < 90%؟
        نعم → 🚨 Red Flag: ابدأ O₂ وأبلغ فورًا
        لا  → تقييم سريع، أبلغ إذا استمر
     لا  → راقب وسجّل
  القراءة مشكوك فيها → أصلح الجهاز أو غيّر موضعه

🌲 تسرع النبض (HR > 100)

قيّم السبب المحتمل: ألم / حمى / قلق / نزيف / جفاف
  HR > 130؟
    نعم → أبلغ فورًا، قيّم BP و SpO₂ وحدد السبب
       توجد أعراض (ألم صدر، ضيق تنفس، دوخة)؟ → طوارئ، استعد لـ ACLS
    لا → راقب كل 30 دقيقة

🌲 ارتفاع الحرارة

Temp > 38°C؟ → أعد القياس → لا يزال > 38°C؟
  نعم → قيّم علامات الجفاف/مصدر العدوى/الأدوية → Temp > 39.5°C؟
     نعم → أبلغ فورًا، قد تحتاج سوائل IV وخافضات، راقب كل ساعة
     لا  → شجع على السوائل وراقب الحرارة
  لا  → سجّل وراقب

👴 اعتبارات كبار السن (> 65 سنة)

  • Orthostatic Hypotension: قس الضغط جالسًا ثم بعد الوقوف بدقيقة — فرق > 20 mmHg SBP يحتاج تقييم.

  • Masked Fever: قد لا يُظهر المسن ارتفاعًا واضحًا في الحرارة حتى مع عدوى شديدة.

  • Lower Baseline Temp: الحرارة الطبيعية قد تكون أقل (36–36.5°C).

  • Atrial Fibrillation: شائع عند المسنين — انتبه لعدم انتظام النبض.

  • Stiff Arteries: قد ترتفع قراءة SBP بسبب تصلب الشرايين مع DBP طبيعي.

  • Reduced Respiratory Reserve: RR > 20 عند المسن يستدعي تقييمًا حتى لو لم يشكُ.

  • SpO₂: قد تكون الطبيعية (93–95%) عند بعض المسنين — راجع Baseline.

  • المسنون أكثر عرضة لتأثيرات الأدوية على العلامات الحيوية.

🤰 اعتبارات الحوامل

  • ضغط الدم: ينخفض في الثلث الأول والثاني ويعود للطبيعي في الثالث.

  • النبض: يرتفع بمعدل 10–20 bpm (Physiological Tachycardia).

  • معدل التنفس: قد يزيد قليلًا بسبب ضغط الرحم على الحجاب الحاجز.

  • درجة الحرارة: طبيعية — الحمى تستدعي تقييمًا عاجلًا لخطرها على الجنين.

  • SpO₂: طبيعية — لكن الحوامل أكثر عرضة لانخفاض O₂ عند الاستلقاء على الظهر.

⚠️ تحذير مهم: BP > 140/90 أثناء الحمل يستدعي تقييمًا فوريًا (قد يكون Pre-eclampsia — التشخيص يحتاج تقييمًا طبيًا كاملًا) → أبلغ الطبيب فورًا ولا تنتظر.

🏥 اعتبارات العناية المركزة (ICU)

  • تكرار القياس: كل ساعة أو بشكل مستمر حسب حالة المريض.

  • Blood Pressure: يُقاس بشكل مستمر عبر Arterial Line في المرضى الحرجين.

  • SpO₂: مراقبة مستمرة مع تسجيل نوع التنفس.

  • Temperature: مراقبة مستمرة — قد يُستخدم Core Temperature Probe.

  • CVP: يُضاف كمؤشر إضافي لتقييم السوائل.

  • MAP: الهدف > 65 mmHg في حالات الصدمة.

  • GCS: يُقيَّم مع كل قراءة علامات حيوية.

  • Urine Output: > 0.5 ml/kg/hr مؤشر على ضخ كافٍ.

MAP = (SBP + 2×DBP) ÷ 3
الهدف في Septic Shock: MAP ≥ 65 mmHg

💎 لآلئ سريرية — Clinical Pearls

🩺 لا تعتمد على رقم واحد فقط — انظر إلى اتجاه القراءات (Trend) مع مرور الوقت.

🩺 إذا بدا المريض مريضًا رغم أن العلامات الحيوية طبيعية — لا تتجاهل ذلك؛ التقييم السريري يتجاوز الأرقام.

🩺 التنفس هو أكثر علامة حيوية يُهمَل قياسها — وهو من أوائل العلامات التي تتغير عند تدهور المريض.

🩺 أي قراءة غير منطقية تستدعي إعادة القياس قبل توثيقها أو اتخاذ قرار.

🩺 NEWS2 ≥ 7 = طوارئ حقيقية — لا تتردد في الاتصال بفريق الاستجابة السريعة.

🩺 الورقة المرجعية — Cheat Sheet

✅ قبل القياس: غسل اليدين (WHO) — التأكد من هوية المريض — شرح الإجراء — تجهيز الأدوات — توفير الخصوصية.

🧠 وسائل الحفظ — Memory Tricks

ترتيب العلامات الحيوية (TPRBS): Temperature – Pulse – Respiration – Blood Pressure – Saturation. جملة للحفظ: "The Patient Requires Blood Support".

تقييم النبض (RRS): Rate – Rhythm – Strength — "Really Regular Strong".

تقييم التنفس (RRDE): Rate – Rhythm – Depth – Effort — "Rapid Rhythms Demand Evaluation".

Red Flags (STOP): Saturation <90% – Tachycardia >130 – O₂ needed urgently – Pressure SBP<90.

SBAR: Situation – Background – Assessment – Recommendation.

أرقام للحفظ السريع: 60–100 (نبض) · 12–20 (تنفس) · 120/80 (ضغط) · 36.5–37.5 (حرارة) · 95–100% (SpO₂) · 65 mmHg (MAP) · 7 (NEWS2 الحرج).

📋 ملخص المراجعة السريعة للامتحان

🎯 أهم 20 نقطة للامتحان:

  1. القيم الطبيعية: T:36.5-37.5(Oral) / P:60-100 / R:12-20 / BP:<120/80 / SpO₂:95-100%

  2. لا تستخدم الإبهام لقياس النبض

  3. انتظر 5 دقائق قبل قياس الضغط

  4. لا تخبر المريض أثناء عدّ التنفس

  5. SpO₂ < 90% = Red Flag (< 92% = تقييم سريع)

  6. قس النبض لمدة 60 ثانية لو غير منتظم

  7. لا تقس الضغط في ذراع بها AV Fistula

  8. قارن دائمًا بالـ Baseline وليس بالقيم العامة فقط

  9. وثّق الوضعية والذراع وموضع الحرارة

  10. غسل اليدين = أول وآخر خطوة دائمًا

  11. MAP ≥ 65 mmHg = الهدف في Septic Shock

  12. NEWS2 ≥ 7 = طوارئ — إبلاغ فوري

  13. qSOFA ≥ 2 = احتمالية Sepsis عالية

  14. Beta Blockers → HR منخفض — قد يكون طبيعيًا

  15. Opioids → RR منخفض — Red Flag إذا < 12

  16. BP > 140/90 أثناء الحمل = تقييم طبي فوري

  17. المسنون قد لا يُظهرون حمى رغم العدوى

  18. التنفس أول علامة تتغير عند التدهور

  19. استخدم SBAR عند الإبلاغ عن أي تدهور

  20. لا تُشخّص ارتفاع أو انخفاض الضغط بقراءة واحدة

❓ الأسئلة الشائعة

هل يجب قياس العلامات الحيوية بنفس الترتيب دائمًا؟
ليس إلزاميًا، لكن يُفضَّل ترتيب ثابت: الحرارة ← النبض ← التنفس ← الضغط ← SpO₂.

ماذا أفعل إذا كانت القراءة غير طبيعية؟
أعد القياس أولًا، ثم قيّم المريض سريريًا، احسب NEWS2، وأبلغ بـ SBAR وفق بروتوكول المنشأة.

ما الفرق بين SpO₂ < 92% و < 90%؟
أقل من 92% يحتاج تقييمًا سريعًا في معظم البالغين، وأقل من 90% Red Flag يستلزم تدخلًا عاجلًا فوريًا.

ما الفرق بين NEWS2 وqSOFA وMEWS؟
NEWS2 أشمل للمرضى العامين بالمستشفى، qSOFA بسيط وسريع للاشتباه بالإنتان خارج ICU، وMEWS أقدم نسبيًا لكن لا يزال يُستخدم في بعض المنشآت.

⭐ أهم النقاط — Key Takeaways

✔ العلامات الحيوية هي أساس التقييم التمريضي وأول خطوة في استقبال أي مريض.

✔ القراءة الواحدة لا تكفي — اتجاه التغير (Trend) أهم من أي رقم منفرد.

✔ سلامة المريض تأتي أولًا — إذا بدا مريضًا رغم القراءات الطبيعية، قيّمه مجددًا.

✔ التوثيق جزء لا يتجزأ من الرعاية — وثّق الموضع والوضعية والوقت.

✔ التنفس أول ما يتغير عند تدهور المريض — لا تهمله أبدًا.

✔ NEWS2 أداة ضرورية لكل ممرض — تعلّم حسابها وتفسيرها.

✔ راعِ الفئات الخاصة: الأطفال، المسنون، الحوامل، مرضى ICU — لكل منهم اعتبارات مختلفة.

content_en:
🩺 Core Nursing Skill — Evidence Level: A (WHO / AHA / NICE / AACN / Potter & Perry)

⏱ Reading time: 20–25 min · Full study time: ~2 hours · Level: Beginner – Intermediate

🎯 Learning Objectives

By the end of this guide, you will be able to:

  • Define vital signs and identify their five core components.
  • Recall normal ranges for each vital sign in adults and children.
  • Understand the role of vital signs in nursing assessment.
  • Recognize factors that affect the accuracy of readings.
  • Distinguish normal from abnormal readings and identify Red Flags requiring immediate action.
  • Apply the correct measurement technique for each vital sign.
  • Document findings and report abnormal readings using SBAR.
  • Use NEWS2, qSOFA, and MEWS to assess patient deterioration.
  • Account for special considerations in children, older adults, pregnancy, and ICU patients.
  • Understand how common medications affect vital signs.

⚡ Quick Facts — Normal Adult Values

Vital SignNormal ValueWhen to Reassess
🌡️ Temperature36.5 – 37.5 °C (oral)< 35°C or > 38.5°C
❤️ Pulse60 – 100 bpm< 60 or > 100, in clinical context
🫁 Respiratory Rate12 – 20 breaths/min< 12 or > 20
🩸 Blood Pressure< 120/80 mmHg< 90/60 or > 140/90 — per clinical context and facility protocol
🫧 Oxygen Saturation (SpO₂)95 – 100%< 92% needs prompt assessment / < 90% Red Flag

📝 Memorize these values well — they are the most frequently tested in exams and clinical practice.

📊 Evidence-Based Practice

OrganizationRecommendationEvidence Level
🌍 WHOMeasure vital signs on every patient admission and with any change in conditionLevel A
❤️ AHAUse an appropriately sized cuff and let the patient rest 5 minutes before measuring BPLevel A
🏥 NICEUse NEWS2 to track patient deterioration based on vital signsLevel A
🇺🇸 CDCClean vital-sign equipment between patients for infection controlLevel A
🫀 AACNIn ICU, critically ill patients have continuous BP monitoring via an arterial lineLevel B
📋 JNC 8 / ACC-AHA 2017Normal < 120/80 — Elevated 120–129 — HTN Stage 1 ≥ 130/80 mmHgLevel A

📖 Introduction

Vital signs are among the most important indicators nurses rely on to assess a patient's health status, since they reflect the body's core functions and help detect changes or deterioration early.

Whether you work in the emergency department, critical care, medical-surgical units, or outpatient clinics, measuring vital signs is the first step in nursing assessment.

A nurse's role isn't limited to taking measurements — it also includes interpreting results, comparing them against previous readings, reporting abnormal changes promptly, and using early-warning tools like NEWS2 to identify patients at risk of deterioration.

📘 Definition — What Are Vital Signs?

Vital signs are a set of measurements that reflect how efficiently the body's vital organs are functioning. They are used to monitor a patient's health status and detect any changes that may indicate a health problem.

The core vital signs include:

  1. 🌡️ Body Temperature
  2. ❤️ Pulse
  3. 🫁 Respiratory Rate
  4. 🩸 Blood Pressure
  5. 🫧 Oxygen Saturation (SpO₂)

💡 In some healthcare institutions, Pain is considered the sixth vital sign, as it directly affects patient assessment and the care plan.

💙 Why Vital Signs Matter for Nurses

  • Assessing the patient's overall condition.
  • Early detection of clinical deterioration.
  • Monitoring the patient's response to treatment.
  • Providing baseline data to compare against future measurements.
  • Detecting infection, bleeding, or shock at an early stage.
  • Making appropriate decisions about notifying the physician or charge nurse.
  • Calculating Early Warning Scores to guide the level of care.

🫀 Anatomy & Physiology

🧠 Hypothalamus: Regulates body temperature and keeps it within the normal range by controlling heat production and loss.

❤️ Heart: Pumps blood to every part of the body, directly affecting pulse and blood pressure.

🫁 Lungs: Responsible for exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide, thereby affecting respiratory rate and oxygen saturation.

🩸 Blood Vessels: Blood pressure changes with vasodilation or vasoconstriction, as well as with the volume of blood the heart pumps.

📚 Medical Terminology

TermMeaning
FeverElevated body temperature
HypothermiaLow body temperature
TachycardiaFast heart rate
BradycardiaSlow heart rate
TachypneaFast respiratory rate
BradypneaSlow respiratory rate
HypertensionHigh blood pressure
HypotensionLow blood pressure
MAPMean Arterial Pressure
HypoxiaReduced oxygen supply to tissues
Shock IndexHR ÷ SBP, a rapid indicator of hemodynamic instability
EWSEarly Warning Score

🛠️ Required Equipment

EquipmentUse
🌡️ ThermometerMeasuring body temperature
🩸 SphygmomanometerMeasuring blood pressure
🎧 StethoscopeAuscultating Korotkoff sounds during BP measurement
❤️ Watch with second handCounting pulse and respirations
🫧 Pulse OximeterMeasuring oxygen saturation and pulse rate
🧤 Clean glovesAs needed per patient condition
🧴 Alcohol swabsCleaning equipment between patients
📝 Vital signs chart / EHRRecording results immediately

⚠️ Make sure equipment is calibrated and in good working order before use — inaccurate devices can lead to wrong clinical decisions.

📋 Indications

  • ✅ On first patient admission (baseline).
  • ✅ Before and after surgical procedures.
  • ✅ Before and after administering certain medications (e.g., antihypertensives, diuretics, beta blockers).
  • ✅ Whenever there is a sudden change in patient condition.
  • ✅ During fever or suspected infection.
  • ✅ When the patient reports severe pain.
  • ✅ Routinely for inpatients per unit protocol.
  • ✅ As ordered by the physician.

🚫 Contraindications & Precautions

🌡️ Oral temperature — do not use if the patient:

  • Is unconscious
  • Is on high-flow oxygen
  • Had hot or cold drinks in the last 20 minutes
  • Had recent oral or jaw surgery

🩸 Blood pressure — do not measure on an arm with:

  • ❌ An AV fistula
  • ❌ An active IV line
  • ❌ Severe edema
  • ❌ A wound or burn
  • ❌ The same side as a mastectomy

👨‍⚕️ Preparation

StepAction
1️⃣ Hand hygienePer infection-control guidelines
2️⃣ Verify patient identityAt least two identifiers: name + medical record number or date of birth
3️⃣ Explain the procedureInform the patient what you're doing and why, to reduce anxiety
4️⃣ Provide privacyUse a curtain or close the door
5️⃣ Gather equipmentHave everything within reach before starting

🔬 Measurement Procedure

🌡️ 1. Body Temperature

Steps: wash your hands, confirm the type and function of the thermometer, then choose the appropriate site:

SiteRouteNormal ValueNote
MouthOral36.5–37.5°CPrimary reference — wait 20 minutes after drinks
ArmpitAxillary36.0–37.0°C~0.5°C lower than oral
EarTympanic36.5–37.5°CFast and practical — ensure correct probe placement
ForeheadTemporal36.5–37.5°CSuitable for children, quick
RectumRectal37.0–38.0°C~0.5°C higher than oral — the most accurate

⚠️ Normal temperature values differ by measurement route, so always document the site to avoid misinterpretation.

After choosing the site: position the device correctly, wait for it to finish and signal, then read and record the result immediately, noting the site.

❤️ 2. Pulse Assessment

Most common site: ✅ Radial artery.

  1. Have the patient rest their arm on a flat surface.
  2. Place your index and middle fingers over the radial artery. ❌ Never use your thumb (it has its own pulse).
  3. Count for 30 seconds × 2 if regular, or a full 60 seconds if irregular.
  4. Assess three elements: Rate, Rhythm (regular/irregular), Strength (strong/weak/thready).
  5. Record the findings.

🩺 If the pulse is irregular, assess the apical pulse for a full minute and notify the responsible nurse/physician.

🫁 3. Respiratory Rate

  1. After counting the pulse, keep your hand on the patient's wrist so they don't notice you're counting respirations.
  2. Observe the rise and fall of the chest.
  3. Count each inhalation + exhalation as one breath.
  4. Count for 30 seconds × 2 if regular, or 60 seconds if irregular.
  5. Assess four elements: Rate, Rhythm, Depth (shallow/normal/deep), Effort (easy or labored).

🩸 4. Blood Pressure

  1. Let the patient rest for 5 minutes before measuring.
  2. Position the arm at heart level.
  3. Choose an appropriately sized cuff (covering 80% of the upper-arm circumference).
  4. Wrap the cuff 2–3 cm above the antecubital fossa.
  5. Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery.
  6. Inflate the cuff until the pulse disappears, then add 20–30 mmHg more.
  7. Deflate at a rate of 2–3 mmHg per second.
  8. Record: Systolic (first Korotkoff sound), Diastolic (sound disappears), arm used, and patient position.

⚠️ High or low blood pressure should never be diagnosed from a single reading. Always interpret it in the full clinical context and facility guidelines, and compare it against baseline.

🫧 5. Oxygen Saturation (SpO₂)

  1. Ensure the patient's finger is clean and warm.
  2. Remove nail polish if possible.
  3. Attach the pulse oximeter to the finger.
  4. Wait for the reading to stabilize (10–15 seconds).
  5. Record: SpO₂, pulse rate, and type of respiratory support (room air / O₂ / ventilator).

⚠️ < 95%: Warrants follow-up and clinical assessment.

⚠️ < 92%: Needs prompt assessment in most adults.

🚨 < 90%: Red Flag indicating severe hypoxia requiring urgent intervention.

In some patients (e.g., COPD), normal baseline values may be lower — always check the patient's baseline and physician orders.

🔍 Scientific Rationale

StepRationale
Hand hygiene before/afterPrevents cross-infection and protects patient and nurse
Verifying patient identityPrevents recording results for the wrong patient
Explaining the procedureReduces anxiety and improves cooperation, which improves accuracy
5-minute rest before BPPhysical activity or anxiety can transiently raise BP, giving a falsely high reading
Arm at heart levelA raised arm gives a falsely low reading; a lowered arm gives a falsely high one
Correct cuff sizeA narrow cuff overestimates BP; a wide cuff underestimates it
Not using the thumb for pulseThe thumb has its own pulse that can be mistaken for the patient's
Not telling the patient you're counting respirationsPatients may voluntarily change their breathing pattern if aware
Recording results immediatelyPrevents forgetting and reduces documentation errors
60-second count for irregular pulseGives a more accurate count given variable intervals between beats
Documenting the temperature siteNormal values differ by site — accurate documentation prevents misinterpretation

💡 Practical Nursing Tips

💡 Always compare the current reading to the patient's baseline, not just general normal values.

💡 Document the patient's position and temperature site — both affect the reading.

💡 If SpO₂ doesn't match the clinical picture, check that the finger is warm and free of nail polish.

💡 In older adults, watch for orthostatic hypotension — measure BP sitting, then standing.

💡 Respiration is the first vital sign to change with deterioration — never skip it.

💡 Don't take a temperature right after bathing or exercise — wait 20–30 minutes.

💡 A patient on beta blockers may have a normal HR of 55 bpm — check medications before classifying a reading.

📝 Nursing Documentation

Documentation should be: accurate (correct numbers with units), legible, timely (immediately after measurement), using correct units (°C, bpm, mmHg, %), and should note the site and position.

Date: [date]          Time: [time]
Temperature:    37.1°C          (Oral)
Pulse:          78 bpm           (Radial, Regular, Strong)
Respiration:    18 /min          (Regular, Normal Depth, No Effort)
Blood Pressure: 118/76 mmHg     (Left Arm, Sitting)
SpO₂:           98%              (Room Air)
NEWS2 Score:    0                (Low Risk)
Patient:        Stable, no signs of distress.
Nurse:          __________________

🩺 If you repeat a measurement due to an abnormal reading, document both readings and explain why it was repeated.

🦠 Infection Control

StageAction
Before measurementHand hygiene — clean equipment — gloves as needed
During measurementUse a fresh probe cover when required — avoid contaminated surfaces
After measurementClean stethoscope and BP cuff with alcohol swabs — safely dispose of single-use items — wash hands again

⚠️ Safety Precautions

🌡️ Temperature: Never use a mercury thermometer with a child or unconscious patient. Avoid the oral route if the patient is uncooperative.

🩸 Blood pressure: Never measure on an arm with an AV fistula, after mastectomy, or with severe injury.

❤️ Pulse: If the radial pulse can't be palpated, try another appropriate site (carotid, femoral, apical).

🫧 Pulse oximeter: Don't rely on the device alone if the reading doesn't match the clinical picture. Cold extremities or poor circulation reduce accuracy.

❌ Common Mistakes

MistakeEffect on the Reading
Wrong cuff sizeNarrow cuff → falsely high; wide cuff → falsely low
Measuring BP over clothingInaccurate reading
Talking during BP measurementRaises the reading
Using the thumb for pulseMay count the examiner's own pulse
Telling the patient you're counting breathsVoluntarily alters the breathing pattern
Not letting the patient rest before measuringFalsely elevated results
Not documenting results immediatelyRisk of forgetting or error
Not noting the temperature siteMisinterpretation of the result
Relying on a single readingMay not represent the true clinical picture
Ignoring current medicationsMisclassifying a reading (e.g., beta blockers slow the heart rate)

🚨 Treat the patient, not the device. If a reading looks odd but the patient looks well, repeat the measurement and check the equipment before acting on it.

🚨 Red Flags — When to Call the Physician Immediately

⚠️ If you notice any of these signs, notify the physician or charge nurse immediately, without delay.

SignThresholdImmediate Action
🫧 SpO₂< 90%Notify immediately — start O₂ per protocol
🩸 SBP< 90 mmHgLay the patient flat — notify immediately
🩸 SBP> 180 mmHgNotify immediately — do not leave the patient
❤️ HR> 130 bpmAssess the cause — notify immediately
❤️ HR< 40 bpmNotify immediately
🫁 RR> 30/minNotify immediately — monitor the airway
🫁 RR< 8/minNotify immediately
🌡️ Temp> 40°CNotify immediately
🌡️ Temp< 35°CNotify immediately
🧠 GCSSudden dropNotify immediately — emergency

🚨 Rule: If two vital signs change at the same time, this signals rapid deterioration — act immediately.

🔀 Decision Trees

🌲 Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg)

SBP < 90? → Repeat to confirm → Still < 90?
  Yes → Lay patient flat, raise legs → Assess ABCDE (consciousness/skin color/symptoms)
        → Notify physician immediately via SBAR → Start IV access, reassess every 5 min
  No  → Monitor the patient and record the reading

🌲 Low SpO₂ (< 95%)

Check the device first (finger warm? no nail polish? probe stable?)
  Reading reliable → Is it < 92%?
     Yes → Is it < 90%?
        Yes → 🚨 Red Flag: start O₂ and notify immediately
        No  → Prompt assessment, notify if it persists
     No  → Monitor and record
  Reading questionable → Fix the device or change the site

🌲 Tachycardia (HR > 100)

Assess the likely cause: pain / fever / anxiety / bleeding / dehydration
  HR > 130?
    Yes → Notify immediately, assess BP and SpO₂, identify the cause
       Symptoms present (chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness)? → Emergency, prepare for ACLS
    No → Monitor every 30 minutes

🌲 High Temperature

Temp > 38°C? → Repeat → Still > 38°C?
  Yes → Assess for dehydration / source of infection / medications → Temp > 39.5°C?
     Yes → Notify immediately, may need IV fluids and antipyretics, reassess hourly
     No  → Encourage fluids and monitor temperature
  No  → Record and monitor

💊 Medication Effects on Vital Signs

⚠️ Important: always check the patient's medication list before classifying any abnormal reading.

Medication / ClassEffectNursing Note
Beta blockers (metoprolol, atenolol)⬇️ HR — ⬇️ BPHR of 55 may be normal for the patient — don't assume bradycardia immediately
Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, verapamil)⬇️ HR — ⬇️ BPWatch for orthostatic hypotension
ACE inhibitors / ARBs⬇️ BPWatch for orthostatic hypotension, especially in older adults
Diuretics (furosemide)⬇️ BP — may ⬇️ HRMonitor for dehydration and hypotension
Vasopressors (norepinephrine)⬆️ BP — ⬆️ HRIn ICU — continuous BP monitoring
Antipyretics (paracetamol, ibuprofen)⬇️ TempMay mask a fever temporarily
Bronchodilators (salbutamol)⬆️ HR — ⬆️ RR transientlyEffect on HR is usually temporary
Opioids (morphine)⬇️ RR — ⬇️ BPRR < 12 with opioids = immediate alert
Atropine⬆️ HRUsed to treat bradycardia
Digoxin⬇️ HRWatch for bradycardia — toxicity is dangerous

💡 Golden rule: ① check current medications ② check the baseline ③ check the clinical picture — before classifying any abnormal vital sign.

👶 Normal Pediatric Values

Age GroupHR (bpm)RR (/min)SBP (mmHg)Temp (°C)SpO₂
Newborn (0–1 mo)100–16030–6060–9036.5–37.595–100%
Infant (1–12 mo)100–15025–4070–10036.5–37.595–100%
Toddler (1–3 yr)90–15020–3080–11036.5–37.595–100%
Preschool (3–6 yr)80–12020–2580–11536.5–37.595–100%
School age (6–12 yr)70–11015–2085–12036.5–37.595–100%
Adolescent (12–18 yr)60–10012–2090–13036.5–37.595–100%

⚠️ Pediatric normal values differ greatly from adults — never apply adult standards to children.

👴 Considerations for Older Adults (> 65)

  • Orthostatic hypotension: Measure BP sitting, then one minute after standing — a drop > 20 mmHg SBP needs assessment.
  • Masked fever: Older adults may not show an obvious temperature rise even with a severe infection.
  • Lower baseline temperature: Normal temperature may run lower (36–36.5°C).
  • Atrial fibrillation: Common in older adults — watch for an irregular pulse.
  • Arterial stiffness: SBP may rise from stiff arteries while DBP stays normal.
  • Reduced respiratory reserve: RR > 20 in an older adult needs assessment even without complaints.
  • SpO₂: A "normal" of 93–95% may apply to some older adults — always check baseline.
  • Older adults are more sensitive to medication effects on vital signs.

🤰 Pregnancy Considerations

  • Blood pressure: Drops in the first and second trimesters and returns to normal in the third.
  • Pulse: Rises by 10–20 bpm (physiological tachycardia).
  • Respiratory rate: May increase slightly due to the growing uterus pressing on the diaphragm.
  • Temperature: Normal — fever requires urgent assessment due to fetal risk.
  • SpO₂: Normal — but pregnant patients are more prone to desaturation when supine.

⚠️ Important warning: BP > 140/90 during pregnancy requires immediate assessment (possible pre-eclampsia — diagnosis requires full medical evaluation) → notify the physician immediately, don't wait.

🏥 ICU Considerations

  • Frequency: Hourly or continuous depending on patient condition.
  • Blood pressure: Continuously monitored via an arterial line in critically ill patients.
  • SpO₂: Continuous monitoring with documentation of oxygen delivery type.
  • Temperature: Continuous monitoring — may use a core temperature probe.
  • CVP: Added as an extra marker for fluid status.
  • MAP: Target > 65 mmHg in shock states.
  • GCS: Assessed with every set of vital signs.
  • Urine output: > 0.5 mL/kg/hr indicates adequate perfusion.
MAP = (SBP + 2×DBP) ÷ 3
Target in septic shock: MAP ≥ 65 mmHg

📊 Early Warning Scores

📊 NEWS2 — National Early Warning Score 2

The leading tool for early detection of patient deterioration in hospitals.

Parameter3210123

SpO₂ % (Scale 1)≤9192–9394–95≥96———
Supplemental O₂———No (Air)—Yes—

📊 qSOFA — Quick SOFA

A rapid tool for identifying sepsis outside the ICU. Criteria (1 point each): RR ≥ 22/min, any altered mental status, SBP ≤ 100 mmHg.

qSOFA ≥ 2 = high likelihood of sepsis → notify the physician immediately and review the full sepsis workup.

📊 MEWS — Modified Early Warning Score

Based on SBP, HR, RR, temperature, AVPU, and urine output. MEWS ≥ 5 = risk of deterioration, notify immediately.

🎯 Clinical Scenario

During morning rounds, you notice a patient (a 70-year-old man admitted with pneumonia) looking pale and complaining of dizziness.

Readings: Temp 37.0°C (normal) — Pulse 118 bpm (tachycardic) — RR 24/min (tachypneic) — BP 88/54 mmHg (hypotensive 🚨) — SpO₂ 94% on room air (low) — Alert but anxious.

NEWS2 = 7 🚨 (very high risk) | qSOFA = 2 (high likelihood of sepsis)

What should the nurse do? Don't leave the patient, call for help immediately, start ABCDE, lay the patient flat and raise the legs, give O₂ per protocol, notify the physician immediately using SBAR, consider transfer to ICU/HDU, and document everything with exact timing.

🎓 Quick Review

SignNormalRed Flag
🌡️ Temp36.5–37.5°C>40 or <35
❤️ Pulse60–100 bpm>130 or <40
🫁 RR12–20/min>30 or <8
🩸 BP<120/80SBP<90 or >180

🧠 Memory Aids (Mnemonics)

  • TPRBS: "The Patient Requires Blood Support" — Temperature, Pulse, Respiration, Blood pressure, Saturation.
  • RRS for pulse: "Really Regular Strong" — Rate, Rhythm, Strength.
  • RRDE for respiration: "Rapid Rhythms Demand Evaluation" — Rate, Rhythm, Depth, Effort.
  • STOP for Red Flags: Saturation <90% — Tachycardia >130 — O₂ needed urgently — Pressure SBP <90.
  • SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.

📋 OSCE Checklist

  • ☐ Hand hygiene
  • ☐ Introduce yourself to the patient
  • ☐ Verify patient identity (two identifiers)
  • ☐ Explain the procedure and obtain consent
  • ☐ Provide privacy
  • ☐ Gather required equipment
  • ☐ Measure temperature correctly, noting the site
  • ☐ Measure pulse (no thumb, correct duration, Rate+Rhythm+Strength)
  • ☐ Measure respirations without telling the patient (Rate+Rhythm+Depth+Effort)
  • ☐ Measure BP, noting arm and patient position
  • ☐ Measure SpO₂ (clean finger, wait for stability)
  • ☐ Record all results immediately
  • ☐ Clean equipment and wash hands afterward
  • ☐ Report any abnormal reading

⭐ Key Takeaways

✔ Vital signs are the foundation of nursing assessment and the first step with any patient.

✔ A single reading isn't enough — the trend over time matters more than any one number.

✔ Patient safety comes first — if a patient looks unwell despite normal readings, reassess.

✔ Documentation is part of care — record site, position, and time.

✔ Respiration is the first sign to change with deterioration — never neglect it.

✔ NEWS2 is an essential tool for every nurse — learn to calculate and interpret it.

✔ Consider special populations: children, older adults, pregnant patients, ICU patients — each has different considerations.

❓ FAQ

Do vital signs need to be measured in the same order every time?
Not mandatory, but a consistent order is preferred: temperature → pulse → respiration → BP → SpO₂.

What should I do if a reading is abnormal?
Repeat the measurement first, assess the patient clinically, calculate NEWS2, and report using SBAR per facility protocol.

What's the difference between SpO₂ < 92% and < 90%?
Below 92% needs prompt assessment in most adults; below 90% is a Red Flag requiring urgent intervention.

What's the difference between NEWS2, qSOFA, and MEWS?
NEWS2 is the most comprehensive and used for general inpatients, qSOFA is a quick sepsis screen outside ICU, and MEWS is an older tool still used in some facilities.
